title: Luke
subtitle: All Twenty-Four Chapters - Key Notes, Cross-References, and Prophecy Fulfilled (WEB)

items.value: This book walks through all twenty-four chapters of Luke, one chapter at a time, with the full text of every chapter printed in it. It grew out of a series of study guides written for a group working through Luke three chapters a week, and it is the fifth volume in this series.

Luke is the longest book in the New Testament, and the only Gospel with a sequel. It opens with four verses of formal Greek addressed to a named reader, in the manner of a Greek historian presenting his credentials, and then drops immediately into an old priest going mute in the temple. That combination - a careful investigator writing about things that cannot be investigated in the ordinary way - is the book in miniature.
It is a companion to the Jeremiah, Matthew, Malachi and Mark volumes in this series, and it is built the same way. If you have used any of those, everything here will be familiar.

The prose is the point. The tables and footnotes are apparatus - useful, and worth using - but they exist to serve a reading of Luke, not to replace one. If you only ever read the chapter introductions and the scripture text, you will have read this book properly.

sections.heading: How this book is put together

items.value: Every chapter follows the same shape.

values: **Key Notes** - the observations worth having in hand before you read: a word that carries more than the translation shows, a custom the first readers took for granted, a connection to something earlier in the book. Each note ends with the verses it comes from.
**Key Cross-References** - eight passages that stand behind or alongside the chapter, grouped by theme.
**Prophecy Fulfilled** - six or seven places where the chapter runs back into the Hebrew Scriptures. The heading is shared with the Matthew and Mark volumes, and there is a caveat about it below.
**For Further Study** - three places to go deeper, from three different traditions.
**Introduction** - the chapter read as a whole before you read it in parts.
**The chapter itself**, printed in full in the World English Bible, with footnote markers on the verses the references belong to.

items.value: Every scripture reference in the book is a live link to the World English Bible on BibleGateway. In the interactive edition, hovering over a footnote marker shows the full text of the passages cited and a line on why they connect, so you can follow a cross-reference without losing your place.

sections.heading: A note on the second table

items.value: The second table in each chapter is headed **Prophecy Fulfilled**, the same as in the Matthew and Mark volumes, so that anyone reading across the Gospels is not relearning the apparatus halfway through.

Luke sits somewhere between the other two on this. He does not use Matthew's explicit formula - "that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet" - anything like as often. But he does something the others do not: he ends the book by making fulfillment the interpretive key to the whole thing. On the road to Emmaus, "beginning from Moses and from all the prophets, he explained to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself," and in the closing scene, "all things must be fulfilled which are written in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms, concerning me."

So Luke's claim is broader rather than narrower. He is not pointing at a dozen proof texts; he is saying the entire Hebrew Scriptures are about this. The table in each chapter is one small instalment of that argument.

sections.heading: A note on the divine names

items.value: In the notes and introductions this book uses **Yahweh** for the covenant name of God and **Yahshua** for the Messiah, as the group this material was written for does.

The printed scripture text is never altered. The World English Bible reads Jesus in the Gospels, and it stands exactly as the translators set it. So you will see Yahshua in a paragraph of commentary and Jesus in the verse beneath it. That is deliberate, and it is not a claim that one is a better translation of the Greek. It simply keeps our own speech and the translator's work visibly distinct.

sections.heading: A note on the chapter titles

items.value: The chapter titles in this book are not traditional and are not found in any Bible. They were written for this study - they name what struck us in that chapter rather than summarising it. Nobody should take them as headings the text itself supplies.

sections.heading: A note on the disputed passages

items.value: Three passages in Luke are missing from some early manuscripts, and two of them are among the best known verses in the Gospel. This book prints all three, as the World English Bible does, and says plainly where the question lies.

**Luke 9:55-56** - "You don't know of what kind of spirit you are. For the Son of Man didn't come to destroy men's lives, but to save them." Spoken after James and John offer to call fire down on a Samaritan village. Many manuscripts have only the bare rebuke and stop there. The sentiment is thoroughly Lukan either way, which cuts both directions: it is exactly what a copyist familiar with this Gospel might have supplied, and exactly what Luke would have written.

**Luke 22:43-44** - the angel strengthening Him in Gethsemane, and the sweat like great drops of blood. Absent from several of the earliest and best manuscripts, present in many others, and quoted by writers in the second century. Some scholars think a scribe added it; others think a scribe removed it, because a Messiah needing angelic help was awkward to defend in the arguments of that era. The evidence genuinely runs both ways.

**Luke 23:34** - "Father, forgive them, for they don't know what they are doing." Missing from an early group of manuscripts, present in most. The same two explanations are offered, and the same honest answer applies: nobody can prove it either way from the manuscripts alone.

This book takes no position on either. It prints them because the WEB prints them, footnotes the evidence at the verse, and leaves the judgment where it belongs. Quietly dropping a verse people know by heart causes far more confusion than a footnote ever has.

sections.heading: Who wrote it, and for whom

items.value: The book is anonymous, but the tradition attaching it to Luke is early and unanimous, and it has an odd feature that argues for it: Luke is a minor figure. He is named three times in the whole New Testament. If a later church were inventing an author for a Gospel this important, it would not have picked him.

Paul calls him "the beloved physician," and lists him among his fellow workers. In the second half of Acts the narration slips into "we" for several stretches - the sea voyage to Philippi, the journey to Jerusalem, the shipwreck on the way to Rome - which reads most naturally as the author saying he was there.

He is almost certainly a Gentile, which would make him the only Gentile writer in the Bible. And he writes for one - Theophilus, addressed as "most excellent," a form of address used for officials. Whoever Theophilus was, Luke expects him to need Roman dates, Greek geography, and explanations of Jewish practice that Matthew would never bother to give.

sections.heading: The prologue, and what it claims

items.value: The first four verses are a single sentence of polished Greek - by common consent the best Greek in the New Testament - and they are the only place in the Gospels where the author steps forward and explains his method.

He says three things. Others have written accounts before him. Those accounts go back to eyewitnesses. And he has traced the course of everything accurately from the first, in order to write it down in order, so that his reader may know the certainty of what he has been taught.

That is a historian's claim, made in a historian's language. It does not settle what you make of the contents - a careful investigator can still be wrong - but it does tell you what kind of book Luke thought he was writing. He was not writing a devotional or a legend. He was writing a report.
Luke is built around a journey, and the journey has a hinge verse: "he steadfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem."

Before that, the ministry is in Galilee. After it, for ten straight chapters, everything happens on a road that is going one place. That travel section is where most of the material unique to Luke sits - the Good Samaritan, the prodigal son, the rich man and Lazarus, the persistent widow, Zacchaeus in the tree. Almost half of this Gospel appears in no other.
Then Jerusalem, and the last week, and a resurrection chapter that ends where the book began - in the temple, with people blessing God.
Every Gospel writer chooses what to include. Luke's choices fall into a pattern that is hard to miss once you see it.

values: **The outsiders.** Shepherds hear it first. A Samaritan is the hero of the parable, and a Samaritan is the one leper who comes back. Tax collectors and sinners keep turning up at the table, and the religious keep objecting.

**Women.** Elizabeth, Mary, Anna, the widow of Nain, the woman with the alabaster jar, Mary and Martha, the women who funded the ministry out of their own money, the women at the tomb. Luke names them and gives them speech.
**Prayer.** Luke shows Yahshua praying at moments the other Gospels pass over - at His baptism, before choosing the twelve, before the first prediction of the cross, at the Transfiguration.
**The Holy Spirit.** More references than Matthew and Mark combined, and most of them in the first four chapters.
**Money.** Luke is the bluntest of the four about wealth, and he does not soften it. The Magnificat has the rich sent away empty before the book is fifty verses old.

items.value: Acts ends with Paul under house arrest in Rome and no verdict, which is a strange place to stop if the author knew how it turned out. That has persuaded many that Acts was finished around AD 62, and Luke therefore somewhat earlier.

Others place it after AD 70, largely on the strength of how specifically chapter 21 describes the fall of Jerusalem. Readers who take predictive prophecy seriously will not find that decisive, and this book does not try to settle it.
Read Luke straight through before any of the apparatus. It is long - allow an evening - but the journey structure only shows if you travel it in one go.
After that, take a chapter at a time. Read the introduction first, then the chapter itself, and come back to the notes and tables afterward; they will mean more once the text is in you.
If you are reading with others, the introductions are written to be read aloud. That is what they were for originally, and they still work best that way.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 1 - A Historian's Preface, Two Impossible Pregnancies, and Two Songs
chapters.title: A Historian's Preface, Two Impossible Pregnancies, and Two Songs
keyNotes: The first four verses are one sentence in Greek, and by common agreement the finest Greek in the New Testament. It is the only place in the Gospels where the author steps out and explains his method (Luke 1:1-4).
"Many have undertaken" tells us Luke was not first, and did not claim to be. He is one witness among several, writing on purpose (Luke 1:1).
"Having traced the course of all things accurately from the first" - parakoloutheo, to follow alongside. The claim is investigation, not private revelation (Luke 1:3).

"Most excellent Theophilus" uses a form of address given to officials. The name means lover of God, which has made some read it as a stand-in for any reader; Luke's own usage suggests a real man (Luke 1:3).
The last word of the sentence in Greek is asphaleia - certainty, safety, firm footing. That is what the whole book is for (Luke 1:4).
The priestly divisions come from 1 Chronicles 24; Abijah is the eighth of twenty-four. Each division served two weeks a year (Luke 1:5).
With thousands of priests and one incense offering a day, burning incense was a once-in-a-lifetime lot, and many never drew it. Zacharias is having the biggest day of his career (Luke 1:9).
The names carry the story: Zacharias is Yahweh remembers, Elizabeth is my God is an oath, and John is Yahweh is gracious (Luke 1:5, 13).
Verse 6 says they were righteous and blameless. Verse 7 says they had no child. Luke puts them in that order deliberately, so nobody can read the childlessness as a verdict (Luke 1:6-7).

Gabriel is named in only one other place in the whole Bible - Daniel, where he explains the seventy weeks. The angel who gave the timetable comes back to say the time is up (Luke 1:19, Daniel 9:21-24).
"No wine nor strong drink" is Nazirite language, and being filled with the Spirit from the womb is not (Luke 1:15, Numbers 6:3).

"To turn the hearts of the fathers to the children" quotes the last two verses of Malachi - the final words of the Old Testament. The New Testament picks up the sentence the Old one stopped on (Luke 1:17, Malachi 4:5-6).

Zacharias and Mary both ask a question, and only one is disciplined. He asks how he can be sure - he wants a guarantee. She asks how it will happen - she wants a mechanism. The difference is not politeness (Luke 1:18, 34).
Being struck mute is a strange punishment until you notice it is also a sign. He asked for one and got one (Luke 1:20).
Betrothal was legally binding and could only be ended by divorce, which is why Mary's situation is dangerous and not merely awkward (Luke 1:27).
"Highly favored" is kecharitomene - a perfect passive participle, one who has been graced. The grammar puts the action on God's side (Luke 1:28).
Verses 32 and 33 hand a peasant girl in an unimportant town the whole of the promise made to David - the throne, the house of Jacob, and a reign with no end (Luke 1:32-33, 2 Samuel 7:12-16).
"Overshadow" is episkiazo, the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the cloud settling on the tabernacle. The vocabulary is Presence vocabulary (Luke 1:35, Exodus 40:34-35).

"Nothing spoken by God is impossible" is almost word for word what was said to Sarah about Isaac. The angel answers a question about a womb with the last answer given about a womb (Luke 1:37, Genesis 18:14).
"Behold, the servant of the Lord" - doule, a female slave. It is not a decorative word (Luke 1:38).
The verb for the baby leaping is the one the Greek Old Testament uses for the twins struggling inside Rebekah. Luke is not describing an ordinary kick (Luke 1:41, Genesis 25:22).
Elizabeth calls Mary "the mother of my Lord" - the first human being in this Gospel to say who the child is, and she does it while He is an embryo (Luke 1:43).
"Blessed is she who believed" blesses the faith rather than the womb, which is exactly the correction Yahshua makes Himself later in the book (Luke 1:45, 11:27-28).
The Magnificat is stitched almost entirely out of the Hebrew Scriptures, and its nearest model is Hannah's song - another woman, another impossible child (Luke 1:46-55, 1 Samuel 2:1-10).
Every verb for what God does in the song is past tense. He has scattered, has put down, has filled, has sent away. Nothing has visibly happened yet (Luke 1:51-53).
"He has put down princes from their thrones" is sung in a country run by Herod on behalf of Rome. This is not a gentle song (Luke 1:52).
Naming happened at circumcision on the eighth day, and naming for the father was expected. Elizabeth breaks the expectation and the neighbours appeal over her head (Luke 1:59-62).
Zacharias's tongue is freed the moment he writes down the name he was given. Speech returns on the far side of agreement (Luke 1:63-64).
The Benedictus reaches for the covenant rather than the child: a horn of salvation in David's house, the oath sworn to Abraham, the holy covenant remembered (Luke 1:68-75).
"The dawn from on high" is anatole, which means sunrise and is also the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the Branch. Both meanings are alive in the line (Luke 1:78, Jeremiah 23:5).
Thirty years disappear into verse 80. Luke does the same thing to Yahshua's childhood in the next chapter (Luke 1:80).

intro: Mark opens with one sentence and a man in the desert. Luke opens with a paragraph that sounds as though it were drafted by a lawyer. The first four verses are a single sentence in Greek, and readers who work in that language generally call it the finest Greek in the New Testament. Luke does what none of the other three do: he stops, speaks in his own voice, and describes his method. Others have compiled accounts. Those accounts go back to eyewitnesses. And he has traced the whole thing accurately from the beginning, in order, so that his reader may know the certainty of what he has been taught. Certainty is the last word of the sentence in Greek, and it is the reason the book exists.

Having established his credentials, he moves immediately into a scene no amount of investigation could have produced: an old priest alone in the sanctuary. There were thousands of priests, twenty-four divisions, and one incense offering a day. The lot to burn incense fell to a man once in a lifetime, if ever. This is the largest day of Zacharias's working life, the crowd is outside praying, and there is an angel standing at the right side of the altar.

Two questions are asked in this chapter and they look identical. Zacharias asks how he can be sure of this; he wants a guarantee before he moves. Mary asks how this can be, since she is a virgin; she has already moved and wants to know the mechanism. One of them goes silent for nine months. The other is given an explanation. The difference between them is not the wording but the direction the question is facing.

What the angel says about John is the last thing the Old Testament said before it stopped. The spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, is the closing sentence of Malachi, and four hundred years later Luke picks the thought up mid-line, as though nothing had been interrupted but the speaking.

Then Gabriel goes to Nazareth, a town so unimportant it is never named in the Hebrew Scriptures, and hands a teenage girl the promise made to David a thousand years earlier - the throne of his father David, the house of Jacob forever, a kingdom with no end. Her answer uses the word doule, a female slave. Behold, the slave of the Lord. It is not a sentimental line, and it was never meant to be a soft one.

Elizabeth, given no information about Mary at all, is the first human being in this Gospel to identify who He is, and she does it before He is born. And Mary's song is not a lullaby. He has scattered the proud, put down princes, sent the rich away empty - sung under Herod, in an occupied country, by someone with nothing, and every verb of it in the past tense. She sings about it as a thing already done while she is three months pregnant and nothing has visibly changed. That is what faith sounds like in this book. The chapter closes with an old man getting his voice back on the far side of obedience, and speaking about a sunrise.

verses.1: Since many have undertaken to set in order a narrative concerning those matters which have been fulfilled among us,
verses.2: even as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and servants of the word delivered them to us,
verses.3: it seemed good to me also, having traced the course of all things accurately from the first, to write to you in order, most excellent Theophilus;
verses.4: that you might know the certainty concerning the things in which you were instructed.
verses.5: There was in the days of Herod, the king of Judea, a certain priest named Zacharias, of the priestly division of Abijah. He had a wife of the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth.
verses.6: They were both righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord.
verses.7: But they had no child, because Elizabeth was barren, and they both were well advanced in years.
verses.8: Now while he executed the priest’s office before God in the order of his division,
verses.9: according to the custom of the priest’s office, his lot was to enter into the temple of the Lord and burn incense.
verses.10: The whole multitude of the people were praying outside at the hour of incense.
verses.11: An angel of the Lord appeared to him, standing on the right side of the altar of incense.
verses.12: Zacharias was troubled when he saw him, and fear fell upon him.
verses.13: But the angel said to him, “Don’t be afraid, Zacharias, because your request has been heard, and your wife, Elizabeth, will bear you a son, and you shall call his name John.
verses.14: You will have joy and gladness; and many will rejoice at his birth.
verses.15: For he will be great in the sight of the Lord, and he will drink no wine nor strong drink. He will be filled with the Holy Spirit, even from his mother’s womb.
verses.16: He will turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord, their God.
verses.17: He will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, ‘to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children,’ and the disobedient to the wisdom of the just; to prepare a people prepared for the Lord.”
verses.18: Zacharias said to the angel, “How can I be sure of this? For I am an old man, and my wife is well advanced in years.”
verses.19: The angel answered him, “I am Gabriel, who stands in the presence of God. I was sent to speak to you, and to bring you this good news.
verses.20: Behold, you will be silent and not able to speak, until the day that these things will happen, because you didn’t believe my words, which will be fulfilled in their proper time.”
verses.21: The people were waiting for Zacharias, and they marveled that he delayed in the temple.
verses.22: When he came out, he could not speak to them, and they perceived that he had seen a vision in the temple. He continued making signs to them, and remained mute.
verses.23: When the days of his service were fulfilled, he departed to his house.
verses.24: After these days Elizabeth, his wife, conceived, and she hid herself five months, saying,
verses.25: “Thus has the Lord done to me in the days in which he looked at me, to take away my reproach among men.”
verses.26: Now in the sixth month, the angel Gabriel was sent from God to a city of Galilee, named Nazareth,
verses.27: to a virgin pledged to be married to a man whose name was Joseph, of David’s house. The virgin’s name was Mary.
verses.28: Having come in, the angel said to her, “Rejoice, you highly favored one! The Lord is with you. Blessed are you among women!”
verses.29: But when she saw him, she was greatly troubled at the saying, and considered what kind of salutation this might be.
verses.30: The angel said to her, “Don’t be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God.
verses.31: Behold, you will conceive in your womb, and give birth to a son, and will call his name ‘Jesus.’
verses.32: He will be great, and will be called the Son of the Most High. The Lord God will give him the throne of his father, David,
verses.33: and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever. There will be no end to his Kingdom.”
verses.34: Mary said to the angel, “How can this be, seeing I am a virgin?”
verses.35: The angel answered her, “The Holy Spirit will come on you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore also the holy one who is born from you will be called the Son of God.
verses.36: Behold, Elizabeth, your relative, also has conceived a son in her old age; and this is the sixth month with her who was called barren.
verses.37: For nothing spoken by God is impossible.”
verses.38: Mary said, “Behold, the servant of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.” The angel departed from her.
verses.39: Mary arose in those days and went into the hill country with haste, into a city of Judah,
verses.40: and entered into the house of Zacharias and greeted Elizabeth.
verses.41: When Elizabeth heard Mary’s greeting, the baby leaped in her womb, and Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit.
verses.42: She called out with a loud voice, and said, “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb!
verses.43: Why am I so favored, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?
verses.44: For behold, when the voice of your greeting came into my ears, the baby leaped in my womb for joy!
verses.45: Blessed is she who believed, for there will be a fulfillment of the things which have been spoken to her from the Lord!”
verses.46: Mary said, “My soul magnifies the Lord.
verses.47: My spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior,
verses.48: for he has looked at the humble state of his servant. For behold, from now on, all generations will call me blessed.
verses.49: For he who is mighty has done great things for me. Holy is his name.
verses.50: His mercy is for generations of generations on those who fear him.
verses.51: He has shown strength with his arm. He has scattered the proud in the imagination of their hearts.
verses.52: He has put down princes from their thrones. And has exalted the lowly.
verses.53: He has filled the hungry with good things. He has sent the rich away empty.
verses.54: He has given help to Israel, his servant, that he might remember mercy,
verses.55: As he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and his offspring forever.”
verses.56: Mary stayed with her about three months, and then returned to her house.
verses.57: Now the time that Elizabeth should give birth was fulfilled, and she gave birth to a son.
verses.58: Her neighbors and her relatives heard that the Lord had magnified his mercy towards her, and they rejoiced with her.
verses.59: On the eighth day, they came to circumcise the child; and they would have called him Zacharias, after the name of his father.
verses.60: His mother answered, “Not so; but he will be called John.”
verses.61: They said to her, “There is no one among your relatives who is called by this name.”
verses.62: They made signs to his father, what he would have him called.
verses.63: He asked for a writing tablet, and wrote, “His name is John.” They all marveled.
verses.64: His mouth was opened immediately, and his tongue freed, and he spoke, blessing God.
verses.65: Fear came on all who lived around them, and all these sayings were talked about throughout all the hill country of Judea.
verses.66: All who heard them laid them up in their heart, saying, “What then will this child be?” The hand of the Lord was with him.
verses.67: His father, Zacharias, was filled with the Holy Spirit, and prophesied, saying,
verses.68: “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, for he has visited and redeemed his people;
verses.69: and has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David
verses.70: (as he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets who have been from of old),
verses.71: salvation from our enemies, and from the hand of all who hate us;
verses.72: to show mercy towards our fathers, to remember his holy covenant,
verses.73: the oath which he swore to Abraham, our father,
verses.74: to grant to us that we, being delivered out of the hand of our enemies, should serve him without fear,
verses.75: In holiness and righteousness before him all the days of our life.
verses.76: And you, child, will be called a prophet of the Most High, for you will go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways,
verses.77: to give knowledge of salvation to his people by the remission of their sins,
verses.78: because of the tender mercy of our God, whereby the dawn from on high will visit us,
verses.79: to shine on those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death; to guide our feet into the way of peace.”
verses.80: The child was growing, and becoming strong in spirit, and was in the desert until the day of his public appearance to Israel.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 2 - A Census, a Feeding Trough, and an Old Man Ready to Die
chapters.title: A Census, a Feeding Trough, and an Old Man Ready to Die
keyNotes: Luke opens the birth with an emperor and closes it with a boy asking questions in the temple. The frame is deliberately political at one end and deliberately domestic at the other (Luke 2:1, 46).

Caesar Augustus is Octavian, who ended the Roman civil wars and was hailed across the empire as saviour and bringer of peace. Luke uses both of those words in this chapter about somebody else (Luke 2:1, 11, 14).

The Quirinius date is a genuine difficulty and this book will not pretend otherwise. Josephus places a census under Quirinius in AD 6, well after Herod died. Proposals include an earlier term of office, a first enrollment in a series, and reading the Greek as "before Quirinius was governor." Luke is unusually accurate about officials elsewhere, which is what makes this interesting rather than simply an error (Luke 2:2).
Micah said Bethlehem seven centuries earlier, and what actually gets the family there is an imperial tax order (Luke 2:4, Micah 5:2).
"Firstborn" is a legal word about inheritance and consecration. It is not a comment on how many children came after (Luke 2:7).

The word translated inn is kataluma, which Luke uses later for the upper room where the Passover is eaten. The commercial inn in the Good Samaritan is a different word entirely. The picture may be a full family house rather than a slammed door (Luke 2:7, 22:11, 10:34).
The feeding trough appears three times in nine verses. Luke will not let you look away from it (Luke 2:7, 12, 16).
Shepherds worked a trade that made regular temple attendance difficult, and their testimony was not highly regarded. They are the first people told (Luke 2:8).

"Good news of great joy" uses the verb the empire used to announce an imperial birth. Savior, Lord and peace on earth were all Augustus's publicity. Luke puts every one of them over a baby in a barn (Luke 2:10-11, 14).
The sign is not the sky full of angels. The sign is the trough (Luke 2:12).

Verse 14 differs between manuscripts by a single letter - peace among men of good will, or peace, good will toward men. The WEB prints the second. It is a small difference and worth knowing about (Luke 2:14).
"Mary kept all these sayings, pondering them in her heart" is said twice in this chapter, and it is the sort of line that suggests where Luke got the material (Luke 2:19, 51).
Circumcision on the eighth day and purification after forty are both straight out of Leviticus. This family keeps Torah (Luke 2:21-24, Leviticus 12).
The offering is two birds, which Leviticus specifies for those who cannot afford a lamb. Luke tells us the family is poor without saying so (Luke 2:24, Leviticus 12:8).
Simeon is waiting for "the consolation of Israel" and Anna speaks to those waiting for "the redemption of Jerusalem." Two phrases for the same long wait (Luke 2:25, 38).
"Now you are releasing your servant" is the language of a slave being discharged from duty. Simeon is asking to be let go (Luke 2:29).

"A light for revelation to the nations" is said in the temple courts, over a Jewish infant, by a devout Jew quoting Isaiah. The Gentile mission is announced from inside the sanctuary (Luke 2:32, Isaiah 49:6).
"Set for the falling and the rising of many" puts falling first. He is not universally good news in Simeon's account of Him (Luke 2:34).
The sword promised to Mary is the only shadow in the whole birth narrative, and it lands on the mother rather than the child (Luke 2:35).
Anna is from Asher, one of the northern tribes people casually describe as lost. Luke names her tribe on purpose (Luke 2:36).
The twelve-year-old in the temple is the only childhood story in any of the four Gospels, and it is not a miracle story - it is a boy listening and asking questions (Luke 2:46).
"I must be in my Father's house" is literally "in the things of my Father." These are His first recorded words, and they quietly set aside the man standing next to Him (Luke 2:49).
"He was subject to them" covers eighteen years in four words (Luke 2:51).
Verse 52 is very close to what is said about the boy Samuel, another child given to the temple after an impossible birth (Luke 2:52, 1 Samuel 2:26).

intro: The chapter opens with the most powerful man on earth signing a document, and it is about what that document accidentally accomplishes. Caesar Augustus ended a century of Roman civil war. Inscriptions across the empire called him saviour of the world; his birthday was announced as good news; his reign was advertised as peace on earth. Within ten verses an angel will use all three of those words over an infant lying in a feeding trough, and Luke knows exactly what he is doing.

Verse 2 is the most argued-over sentence here. Josephus records a census under Quirinius in AD 6, and Herod died in 4 BC, which puts the two on opposite sides of each other. Proposals include an earlier term of office, a first enrolment in a series, or reading the Greek as before Quirinius was governor. This book does not claim to know which is right. What is worth noting is that Luke is otherwise remarkably careful with titles and officials, which is precisely why the difficulty deserves attention rather than dismissal in either direction.
Micah named Bethlehem seven hundred years earlier. The thing that moves this family the eighty miles to get there is a tax form. That is how God moves through this Gospel - no trumpet, a bureaucrat.

The word translated inn is kataluma, the same word Luke uses later for the upper room where the Passover is eaten. When he means a commercial inn, as in the parable of the Samaritan, he uses an entirely different word. So the scene may not involve a hard-faced innkeeper at all, but a family house so full that the only place to lay a newborn is where the animals feed. Either way Luke says trough three times in nine verses. He wants the reader looking at it.

Shepherds are told first. Their work made regular temple attendance difficult and their word carried little weight in court. And the sign they are given is not the glory or the army of heaven filling the sky; the sign is a baby wrapped up in a feeding trough. The confirmation of the Messiah is that He is somewhere nobody would think to look. At the temple, the offering is two birds - which Leviticus permits only for a family that cannot afford a lamb. Luke never says they were poor. He reports what went on the altar and leaves the arithmetic to the reader.

Simeon has been waiting long enough that death has become the thing he is asking for, and his words are the language of a slave being discharged from duty. He announces over this infant a light for revelation to the nations - a devout Jew, in the sanctuary, saying this is for everybody. Then the only shadow in the entire birth narrative, and it does not fall on the child: a sword will pierce through your own soul. Anna follows, eighty-four years a widow, from the tribe of Asher, one of the ten that people call lost, standing right there. And the chapter ends with the only story from His childhood in any Gospel, and then swallows eighteen years in one sentence: He went down with them and was subject to them.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 3 - Six Rulers, One Word, and a Genealogy Running Backwards
chapters.title: Six Rulers, One Word, and a Genealogy Running Backwards
keyNotes: Verses 1 and 2 date the ministry against six named officials. It is the most precisely dated moment in the Gospels, and it is Luke's historian's habit showing (Luke 3:1-2).

"The fifteenth year of Tiberius" lands somewhere around AD 28 or 29 depending on where you start the count, which is exactly the kind of detail a careful writer includes and a myth-maker does not (Luke 3:1).

"In the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas" names two men for one office. Rome had deposed Annas and installed his son-in-law; many Jews still regarded the office as held for life. Luke records the awkward reality rather than tidying it (Luke 3:2).
"The word of God came to John" is the standard Hebrew prophetic formula. Luke uses it of no one else in this Gospel. He is telling you the prophets are back (Luke 3:2, Jeremiah 1:2).
Matthew and Mark quote two lines of Isaiah 40. Luke keeps going to "all flesh will see God's salvation." The extra line is the reason he is quoting it (Luke 3:6, Isaiah 40:5).
The image of filling valleys and levelling hills is roadworks - the crew that goes ahead of a visiting king to make the route passable (Luke 3:4-5).
In Matthew, "offspring of vipers" is aimed at Pharisees and Sadducees. In Luke it is aimed at the crowds who came out to be baptized. Luke will not let the reader stand at a safe distance (Luke 3:7).
"We have Abraham for our father" is descent used as a defence, and it is taken apart with a pun that only works in Hebrew - stones, abanim, and children, banim (Luke 3:8).
Only Luke records the three answers to "what must we do?" - and not one of the three is told to leave their occupation (Luke 3:10-14).
The crowds are told to share a coat. Repentance in this Gospel starts in a cupboard (Luke 3:11).
Tax collectors are told to collect no more than they are appointed to - which means staying in a despised job and doing it honestly (Luke 3:13).
The soldiers' word for extortion means to shake violently. John names the standard shakedown and tells them to stop, and to be content with their wages (Luke 3:14).

"He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire" is explained by the very next verse: the fire is what happens to the chaff. Two baptisms are on offer, and the winnowing fork decides which (Luke 3:16-17).
The threshing floor image is not gentle. The fan throws everything into the air and lets the wind sort it (Luke 3:17).
Luke reports John's imprisonment before he narrates the baptism, moving John off the stage before Yahshua steps onto it. It is arrangement, not chronology (Luke 3:19-21).
Only Luke has Him praying at His baptism. In this Gospel the heavens open while He prays (Luke 3:21).
"In a bodily form like a dove" - Luke alone insists the descent was visible (Luke 3:22).
The voice combines Psalm 2, spoken over the enthroned king, with Isaiah 42, spoken over the servant who will be crushed. Both titles, in one sentence, before He has done anything (Luke 3:22).
"Being the son (as was supposed) of Joseph" - Luke flags the qualification himself, in the middle of his own genealogy (Luke 3:23).
Matthew's genealogy runs forward from Abraham; Luke's runs backwards from Yahshua. Matthew stops at Abraham; Luke keeps going to Adam (Luke 3:23-38).

The two lists diverge after David - Matthew through Solomon, Luke through Nathan. The old proposals are Mary's line, levirate marriage, or legal against biological descent. This book does not pick one, and neither should anyone pretend the question is settled (Luke 3:31).
A Gentile writer traces a Jewish Messiah past Abraham to the father of everybody. That is the argument of this Gospel done as a list (Luke 3:38).
The last three words of the chapter are "the son of God." The first words of the next are "if you are the Son of God." The chapter break hides a direct hit (Luke 3:38, 4:3).

intro: The chapter opens the way a Roman historian opens a chapter. The fifteenth year of Tiberius, Pilate over Judea, Herod over Galilee, Philip over Ituraea and Trachonitis, Lysanias over Abilene, Annas and Caiaphas in the high priesthood. Six rulers, nailed to a calendar. Luke is saying that this can be checked.

The last pair is odd - two men named for one office. Rome had removed Annas and installed his son-in-law, while a great many Jews still held the high priesthood to be a lifetime appointment, so in practice there were two. Luke does not tidy that up. Writing down the awkward thing is generally the mark of a man reporting rather than arranging.

And then, in the middle of that list of powerful men, the word of God comes to John in the wilderness. That phrase is a formula, not a flourish; it is how the prophetic books begin. Four centuries without it, and it returns in a list of governors and lands on none of them.

Matthew and Mark both quote Isaiah 40 and stop after a line or two. Luke keeps going, and the line he keeps going for is that all flesh will see God's salvation. That is his whole book in four words. The image itself is roadworks - fill the valleys, cut the hills, straighten the bends - the work a crew did before a king came through, and not for an ordinary traveller.

John's preaching is not gentle, and in Luke the vipers are the crowds who came out to be baptized rather than the religious professionals, which removes the safe distance from which a reader might enjoy watching somebody else be told. The defence he dismantles is ancestry - God can raise up children to Abraham from stones, which in Hebrew is a pun on the two words. Then three groups ask the same question, and the question is only in Luke: what shall we do? The answers are almost disappointing. Share a coat. Collect no more than you are appointed to. Do not extort, and be content with your wages. Nobody is told to leave his job. Repentance here happens in a cupboard and a ledger.

The winnowing fork is often read as one lovely promise, but the wheat goes into the barn and the chaff burns, and the fire of one verse is explained by the next. Then the baptism, with a detail only Luke has: Jesus was praying, and while He prayed the sky opened. That will happen repeatedly in this Gospel. And the voice says two things at once - you are my beloved Son, from a psalm about an enthroned king, and in you I am well pleased, from a passage about a servant who is crushed. Crown and cross in a single sentence, before He has healed anybody. Then the genealogy, which runs backwards, past Abraham, past Noah, all the way to Adam, and ends: the son of Adam, the son of God. Turn the page, and the first words spoken to Him put the word if in front of that.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 4 - The Wilderness, a Scroll Handed Back, and a Cliff
chapters.title: The Wilderness, a Scroll Handed Back, and a Cliff
keyNotes: "Full of the Holy Spirit... led by the Spirit into the wilderness." Luke makes the testing Spirit-led rather than devil-initiated. He is not ambushed; He is sent (Luke 4:1).
Forty days in a wilderness with hunger and testing is Israel's forty years compressed. Where the nation failed, He does not (Luke 4:2, Deuteronomy 8:2-3).
All three answers come from Deuteronomy 6 to 8 - the exact passage explaining why Israel was led into the wilderness in the first place. He is not quoting at random (Luke 4:4, 8, 12).
Luke's order differs from Matthew's. Matthew ends on the mountain; Luke ends on the temple in Jerusalem, because in this Gospel everything runs toward Jerusalem (Luke 4:9, Matthew 4:8-10).
The devil claims the kingdoms have been delivered to him, and the claim is not contested. What is refused is the price, not the ownership (Luke 4:6-8).
"He departed from him until another time" - achri kairou, until an opportune moment. Luke picks that thread up again when Satan enters Judas (Luke 4:13, 22:3).
"As was his custom" tells us He was a regular at that synagogue. The people about to throw Him off a cliff had watched Him there for years (Luke 4:16).
Standing to read and sitting to teach was the practice. When He sits down, the sermon is beginning, not ending (Luke 4:16, 20).
The reading is Isaiah 61:1-2 with one line of Isaiah 58:6 folded into the middle of it - "to deliver those who are crushed." That is a deliberate join, not a slip (Luke 4:18).
He stops in the middle of a sentence. Isaiah 61:2 continues "and the day of vengeance of our God," and He closes the scroll before it. The omission is the sermon (Luke 4:19, Isaiah 61:2).
"The acceptable year of the Lord" is Jubilee language: debts cancelled, slaves released, land returned to its families (Luke 4:19, Leviticus 25:10).
"Today, this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing" is the shortest recorded sermon in the Gospels and the most inflammatory (Luke 4:21).
"Isn't this Joseph's son?" is admiration curdling. They are impressed and unwilling at the same time (Luke 4:22).
The turn comes exactly when He mentions Gentiles. Zarephath was in Sidon, and Naaman was a Syrian commander - two foreigners helped while Israelites were not (Luke 4:25-27).
Both examples are chosen for maximum offence, and He chooses them before anyone has thrown anything (Luke 4:25-27, 1 Kings 17:8-16, 2 Kings 5:9-14).

Luke puts the rejection at Nazareth at the very start of the ministry. Matthew and Mark place a similar scene much later. Luke wants it read as the pattern rather than an episode (Luke 4:16-30, Mark 6:1-6).
"Passing through the middle of them, went his way." No explanation is offered, and Luke does not offer one (Luke 4:30).
In Capernaum the demon uses the same words as in Mark, and gets the same answer: be silent (Luke 4:34-35, Mark 1:24-25).
Luke, alone of the four, notes that the demon threw the man down "having done him no harm" - a clinical observation about outcome (Luke 4:35).
"A great fever" is a graded classification. Ancient medical writers distinguished great and small fevers, and Luke uses the term (Luke 4:38).
The fever is rebuked, using the same verb used on the demon a few verses earlier (Luke 4:35, 39).
"He laid his hands on every one of them." Only Luke says every one - no crowd healing at a distance, one person at a time (Luke 4:40).
"I must preach the good news of God's Kingdom" - dei, it is necessary. This little verb runs through Luke like a spine, and it always attaches to God's purpose (Luke 4:43).

intro: Chapter 3 ends with the son of Adam, the son of God. Chapter 4 begins with a voice putting the word if in front of it. The chapter break hides a direct hit, and it is the pattern of the thing: the word comes first, and then something arrives to ask whether it is actually believed.

Notice who does the leading. He is full of the Holy Spirit and led by the Spirit into the wilderness. He is not ambushed there; He is taken on purpose. Forty days, hunger, a wilderness - Israel spent forty years in one, tested with hunger, and Deuteronomy 8 exists to explain why. Every answer He gives comes out of Deuteronomy. He stands in the test the nation failed, quoting the passage written about it, and passes.

One detail in verse 6 deserves attention. The devil claims that all this authority has been delivered to him and that he gives it to whomever he wishes, and the claim is not contradicted. The price is refused; the claim is left standing. And verse 13 is easy to skim: he departed from him until an opportune time. That thread is picked up eighteen chapters later, when Satan enters Judas.

Then Nazareth, and the synagogue He grew up in, where the congregation had watched Him sit every Sabbath for years. He is handed Isaiah and reads the Jubilee text - good news to the poor, release to the captives, sight to the blind, the acceptable year of the Lord. Leviticus 25: debts wiped, slaves released, land returned to the families that lost it.

And then He stops mid-sentence. Isaiah 61:2 continues with the day of vengeance of our God. He reads the first half, rolls the scroll, hands it back and sits down. The vengeance is not cancelled; it is simply not this visit. He closed the book inside a comma, and every person in that room knew the rest of the verse by heart. Then the shortest sermon on record: today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.

At first they are proud of Him. What turns the room is two names - a widow in Sidon and a Syrian army commander, both foreigners, both helped while Israelites were passed over. Admiration becomes a cliff edge in four verses. And Luke has placed this at the very beginning of the ministry, where Matthew and Mark have a similar scene much later, because he wants it read as the pattern rather than an incident. The remainder of the chapter reads like a physician's notes - a great fever, which was an actual medical classification, a demon that did the man no harm on the way out, and hands laid on every single person rather than a wave over a crowd. And when a whole town wants to keep Him, the answer contains the word dei: I must preach the Kingdom to the other cities also. That word runs through this Gospel, and it never once means He felt like it.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 5 - A Boat Borrowed, a Roof Opened, and Wine That Bursts the Skins
chapters.title: A Boat Borrowed, a Roof Opened, and Wine That Bursts the Skins
keyNotes: Luke calls it the lake of Gennesaret rather than the sea of Galilee. He is writing for readers who know Greek geography, and it is a lake (Luke 5:1).
He borrows a pulpit before He calls a disciple. Simon's boat becomes a platform first and a net second (Luke 5:3).
"We worked all night, and took nothing." Night was the productive time for that fishery, so the instruction to fish in daylight in deep water is professionally wrong (Luke 5:4-5).
"But at your word I will let down the net." The whole obedience hangs on that phrase, and Peter offers one net where he was told nets (Luke 5:5).
Peter's response to a miracle of provision is not celebration but confession. Abundance shows him something about himself (Luke 5:8).
"Catching people alive" translates zogreo - to take alive, the word used of sparing captives rather than killing them. Fishing normally ends with a dead fish; this does not (Luke 5:10).
Only Luke tells the call of the fishermen with this catch attached. Matthew and Mark have the call without it (Luke 5:1-11, Mark 1:16-20).
"Full of leprosy" grades the severity - another physician's note (Luke 5:12).
The leper doubts the willingness, not the power: "if you want to." The reply takes his exact word back - "I want to" (Luke 5:12-13).
He touches him. Under the law that transfers uncleanness outward; here it runs the other direction (Luke 5:13, Leviticus 5:3).
Sending him to the priest keeps Torah intact. The healing does not bypass the law it fulfils (Luke 5:14, Leviticus 14:2-4).
"He withdrew himself into the desert, and prayed" is in a tense that means habitually, repeatedly. It is a practice, not an occasion (Luke 5:16).

Luke says tiles; Mark says they dug through the roof. A Galilean farmhouse had a mud-and-branch roof, a Greco-Roman house had tiles. Each writer describes the roof his readers picture (Luke 5:19, Mark 2:4).
"Seeing their faith" is plural. The faith that gets credited belongs to the men carrying the cot (Luke 5:20).
The scribes' theology is correct: only God forgives sins. They hold the right premise and refuse the only conclusion available (Luke 5:21).
This is the first time in Luke that Yahshua calls Himself the Son of Man, and He does it to make a claim about authority (Luke 5:24, Daniel 7:13-14).
Levi is Matthew. Luke gives the tax booth its technical name and does not soften the profession (Luke 5:27).
"He left everything" is Luke's phrase - he uses it of the fishermen and of Levi, and of nobody in the other Gospels (Luke 5:11, 28).
Levi's first act of discipleship is throwing a party and inviting his old colleagues (Luke 5:29).
"I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance." Luke adds those last two words; Matthew and Mark stop at sinners (Luke 5:32, Mark 2:17).
The bridegroom saying carries the first shadow in this Gospel of His being taken away (Luke 5:35).
New cloth on old cloth and new wine in old skins are not arguments for improving the arrangement. They are arguments that it cannot hold this (Luke 5:36-38).
Verse 39 appears only in Luke, and it is wry and a little sad: nobody who has drunk the old wants the new, because the old is comfortable (Luke 5:39).

intro: The chapter opens with a man borrowing a boat, and the detail is easy to walk past. The crowd is pressing in, He needs distance and acoustics, so He gets into Simon's boat and asks him to push out a little. He uses Simon's workplace as a pulpit before He calls Simon to anything at all. The first thing asked of this man is the loan of his tools.

Then the instruction: put out into the deep and let down the nets. Simon is a professional. They fished at night, in the shallows. Daylight and deep water are the wrong time and the wrong place, and a carpenter is telling a fisherman his business. His answer is one of the great sentences in this Gospel - we worked all night and took nothing, but at your word I will let down the net. He states everything true about the situation first, refuses to pretend it makes sense, and does it anyway.

When the nets tear he does not celebrate. He goes down on his knees in a boat filling with fish and asks Him to leave, because he is a sinful man. That is what proximity to holiness produces; Isaiah saw the throne and said he was undone. And the answer is that from now on he will be catching people alive. The Greek word means to take alive, and it is used of sparing prisoners rather than killing them - because fishing normally ends badly for the fish.

The leper's request is precisely worded. He has no doubt about the power and is unsure of the willingness: if you want to, you can make me clean. The answer uses his own word back at him. But before the word there is a hand. Under the law, touching a leper transmitted uncleanness; here it runs the other way entirely. And then the man is sent to the priest to make the offering Moses commanded. The law is not bypassed; it is walked into.
Verse 16 is one sentence and it is the whole ministry: He withdrew into the wilderness and prayed. The tense means it was a habit rather than an occasion. The busier it became, the more He left.

Then a roof comes apart above the teacher's head, and the text says He saw their faith - plural. The man on the mat is never recorded saying anything; he is carried there on somebody else's believing. And the first thing said to him is not what anybody came for. The scribes who object are not being stupid; their premise is correct, and who can forgive sins but God alone is good theology. They have the right premise and will not take the one step it leaves them. Then Levi leaves a tax booth and throws a party, and then the wineskins - which are not a small saying. New wine expands, and a skin that has already stretched as far as it will go splits. The old is not called bad. It is called unable to contain what is coming. And the last verse, which only Luke has, is quietly devastating: no one who has drunk old wine wants new, for he says the old is better.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 6 - Grain on the Sabbath, a Night on the Mountain, and a House Without a Foundation
chapters.title: Grain on the Sabbath, a Night on the Mountain, and a House Without a Foundation
keyNotes: "The second Sabbath after the first" translates a phrase found nowhere else in Greek literature, and nobody is certain what it means. Proposals abound; this book does not pick one (Luke 6:1).
Plucking grain by hand from someone else's field was expressly permitted in Torah. The objection is to the day, not the taking (Luke 6:1-2, Deuteronomy 23:25).
The David defence appeals to a precedent where hunger overrode a ritual restriction, and it involves bread reserved for priests (Luke 6:3-4, 1 Samuel 21:1-6).
"The Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath" claims authority over something God made and commanded. It is a larger statement than the argument required (Luke 6:5).
Only Luke says the withered hand was the right hand - the working hand, the earning hand (Luke 6:6).
They are watching to see whether He will heal, in order to build a charge. The healing is the evidence they are collecting (Luke 6:7).
He makes the man stand in the middle first. Nothing here is done quietly (Luke 6:8).
"Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good, or to do harm? To save a life, or to kill?" - and their answer, two verses later, is to start planning a killing (Luke 6:9, 11).
Only Luke records the all-night vigil before the twelve are chosen. The most consequential personnel decision in history follows a night of prayer (Luke 6:12).
"Whom he also named apostles" - apostolos, one who is sent. Luke uses the word far more often than the other Gospel writers (Luke 6:13).
Simon the Zealot and Matthew the tax collector are on the same list. A nationalist insurgent and a man who worked for Rome, told to travel together (Luke 6:15).

"He came down with them, and stood on a level place." This is the Sermon on the Plain. Whether it is Matthew's sermon from a different angle or a separate occasion is an old question, and this book leaves it open (Luke 6:17, Matthew 5:1).
Luke has four blessings and four matching woes. Matthew has nine blessings and no woes at all (Luke 6:20-26, Matthew 5:3-12).

Luke writes "blessed are you who are poor"; Matthew writes "poor in spirit." Both are printed here as they stand. The difference is real, and flattening it in either direction costs you something (Luke 6:20, Matthew 5:3).
The woes are laments rather than curses. Ouai is a cry of grief, closer to "alas for you" than to a sentence being passed (Luke 6:24-26).
"Woe when men speak well of you" is the hardest verse in the chapter for anybody with an audience (Luke 6:26).
Love your enemies is given four ways in two verses - love, do good, bless, pray - and every one of them is an action rather than a feeling (Luke 6:27-28).
"Give to everyone who asks you" is stated without qualification. Luke does not soften it and neither will this book (Luke 6:30).
Where Matthew has "be perfect as your Father is perfect," Luke has "be merciful as your Father is merciful." Luke names mercy as the family resemblance (Luke 6:36, Matthew 5:48).
"Good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over" describes a grain seller filling the fold of a garment used as a bag (Luke 6:38).
"Everyone when he is fully trained will be like his teacher" is a warning about whose voice you sit under, placed immediately after the blind leading the blind (Luke 6:39-40).
The speck is a splinter of chaff and the beam is a roof timber. The disproportion is meant to be funny, and the laugh is the point (Luke 6:41-42).
"Why do you call me, Lord, Lord, and don't do the things which I say?" is the sermon applying its own test before the parable arrives (Luke 6:46).
Luke's builder "dug and went deep" to reach rock. Matthew's simply builds on it. Luke adds the digging - the unseen work that nobody watching can verify (Luke 6:48, Matthew 7:24-25).

further.desc: exposition of the grain fields, the withered hand, and the Sabbath question

intro: Two Sabbath arguments open the chapter and they escalate quickly. In the first, the disciples pull heads of grain and rub them in their hands. Nobody is accusing them of theft; Deuteronomy explicitly permits plucking grain by hand from a neighbour's field, provided no sickle is used. The objection is the day. Rubbing looked like threshing, and threshing was work.

The answer goes to David eating the show bread, which was strictly not lawful for him - the argument being that need has always been allowed to bend ritual, and that the precedent sits in the middle of the story of Israel's greatest king. And then a claim far larger than the argument required: the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath. That is not a statement about grain. The Sabbath is something God made and commanded; to be lord of it is to be over it.

The second Sabbath brings a man with a withered hand, and the physician tells us which hand - the right one, the working one. They are watching to see whether He will heal, so that they can bring a charge. So He makes it maximally public, stands the man in the middle, and asks whether the Sabbath is for saving life or destroying it. The answer they give is to fill with rage and begin discussing what they might do to Him. He asked whether the day was for saving or killing, and they answered by plotting a murder on it.

Then the mountain, and a line only Luke has: He continued all night in prayer to God. In the morning He picks twelve. The most consequential staffing decision in history follows a night alone on a hill. And the list contains Simon the Zealot, from the nationalist resistance that wanted Rome driven out by force, and Matthew, who collected Rome's taxes. In almost any other setting one of those men would have knifed the other. They are put on the same team and sent out together.

He comes down and stands on a level place - not up a mountain but down on the flat, inside the crowd - and preaches a shorter, sharper sermon than Matthew's. Four blessings and four woes. Matthew has poor in spirit and hungering for righteousness; Luke simply has poor, and hungry now. The difference is really there, and this book will not smooth it over. Luke is the writer who refuses to let wealth become a metaphor. And the woes are cried in grief rather than spat in anger - the word is closer to weeping than to cursing - including the one that should stop anybody who has ever wanted to be liked: woe to you when all men speak well of you.

Love of enemies is given as four verbs and not as a feeling - love, do good, bless, pray - all of them things done whether or not the feeling arrives. Where Matthew closes that section with be perfect as your Father is perfect, Luke closes it with be merciful as your Father is merciful. Same family, different word for the resemblance. The speck and the beam is a joke and is meant to land as one: a splinter of chaff, a roof timber, and a man with a rafter in his eye offering eye surgery. And the chapter ends with two houses and one storm. Luke adds what Matthew does not - his builder dug, and went deep, and laid a foundation on rock. The digging is the part of the work that is underground, takes the longest, and cannot be seen at all, because on a clear day the two houses look identical.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 7 - A Centurion's Message, a Coffin Stopped, and a Woman Who Would Not Stop Crying
chapters.title: A Centurion's Message, a Coffin Stopped, and a Woman Who Would Not Stop Crying
keyNotes: In Luke the centurion never meets Yahshua. He sends two delegations - Jewish elders first, then friends. In Matthew he comes himself. Luke keeps the distance, which is the point of the story (Luke 7:3, 6, Matthew 8:5).
The elders say "he is worthy." The centurion says "I am not worthy." Two verdicts on the same man, reached from opposite directions (Luke 7:4, 6).

"He built our synagogue for us" - a Roman officer paying for Jewish worship. God-fearers, Gentiles who attached themselves to the synagogue without converting, were common, and Luke will fill Acts with them (Luke 7:5).
"I also am a man placed under authority" is the whole argument. He reasons that Yahshua, like himself, stands inside a chain of command - which is why a word at a distance would be enough (Luke 7:8).
"He marveled at him." There are only two things in the Gospels said to astonish Yahshua: this man's faith, and unbelief at Nazareth (Luke 7:9, Mark 6:6).
Nain is a small town about six miles from Nazareth, and this is the only mention of it in Scripture (Luke 7:11).
The dead man is the only son of a widow. That is two losses in one - her child, and the last person legally obliged to provide for her (Luke 7:12).
"He had compassion on her" - splagchnizomai, a word about the gut. And note the object: the compassion is aimed at the mother, not the corpse (Luke 7:13).
"Don't cry" is a terrible thing to say at a funeral unless you can do something about it (Luke 7:13).
He touches the bier. Under Numbers 19 contact with the dead makes a man unclean for seven days. This is the third time in this Gospel He touches what defiles (Luke 7:14, Numbers 19:11).

"He gave him to his mother" is word for word what is said of Elijah at Zarephath. And Nain sits a couple of miles from Shunem, where Elisha raised another woman's only son (Luke 7:15, 1 Kings 17:23, 2 Kings 4:36).
"God has visited his people" uses the verb Zacharias used in the Benedictus. The word has been waiting since chapter 1 (Luke 7:16, 1:68).
John's question comes from prison, and Luke does not soften it. The man who saw the dove and heard the voice is asking whether he backed the right person (Luke 7:19).

The answer is assembled from Isaiah 35 and Isaiah 61 - and one promised item is conspicuously missing. Isaiah 61 also promises liberty to the captives, and the man asking is in a cell (Luke 7:22, Isaiah 61:1).
"Blessed is he who finds no occasion for stumbling in me" is spoken directly to a man whose expectations are not being met (Luke 7:23).
"A reed shaken by the wind" may have teeth: Herod Antipas minted coins stamped with a reed, and it is Herod who has John in prison (Luke 7:24).
"He who is least in God's Kingdom is greater than he" is a statement about position in a new order, not a mark against John's character (Luke 7:28).
Verses 29 and 30 are Luke's own aside to the reader. The people and the tax collectors declared God just; the Pharisees and lawyers "rejected the counsel of God" for themselves (Luke 7:29-30).

The children in the marketplace will not play weddings or funerals. John fasted and was called demon-possessed; Yahshua ate and was called a drunk. The objection was never really about the diet (Luke 7:31-34).

This is not the anointing at Bethany. Luke places it early, in Galilee, at a Pharisee's table, and the woman is unnamed. Identifying her with Mary Magdalene is a tradition that starts centuries later and has nothing in the text behind it (Luke 7:37, Mark 14:3).
She lets her hair down in a room full of men, which in that culture was shocking, and she does it before she has been forgiven anything in the narrative (Luke 7:38).
Simon's failure is entirely in what he did not do: no water for the feet, no kiss of greeting, no oil. Ordinary courtesies, all omitted (Luke 7:44-46).

"Her sins are forgiven, for she loved much" reads backwards if you take it alone - but the parable set immediately before it makes love the result of being forgiven, not the payment for it (Luke 7:41-47).
The last word is "your faith has saved you," not your love. Luke will not let the point blur (Luke 7:50).

further.desc: exposition of the centurion's faith and the two delegations he sends

intro: Two people are praised in this chapter and neither is a religious professional. One is an officer in an occupying army; the other is a woman everybody in the room knows by reputation.

Luke does something with the centurion that Matthew does not: the man never appears. He sends Jewish elders, then he sends friends, and the two never meet. And the chapter records two verdicts on him that point in opposite directions. The elders say he is worthy, because he loves the nation and built the synagogue. He sends word that he is not worthy to have Him under his roof. His reasoning is a soldier's - I am a man under authority, I say go and he goes, so you need not be in the room, only say the word. There are two things recorded as astonishing Yahshua in the Gospels: this man's faith, and the unbelief of His own home town.

At Nain a funeral procession comes out of the gate as He is going in, and the dead man is the only son of a widow. Her husband is already gone; this was the one person legally responsible for keeping her fed. She is not only grieving, she has just become destitute. And the text says He had compassion on her - not on him, on her. Then He touches the bier, which under Numbers makes Him unclean for a week. He has already touched a leper two chapters earlier, and He keeps doing this.

He gave him to his mother is a quotation. Elijah raised a widow's son at Zarephath and delivered him with those words, and Nain sits a couple of miles from Shunem, where Elisha did the same for another woman's only child. When the crowd says a great prophet has arisen, they are not being vague; they are naming the two prophets whose territory this is.

Then the hardest thing in the chapter. John sends a question from prison: are you the one who is coming, or should we look for another? This is the man who leapt in the womb, who saw the Spirit descend, who called Him the Lamb of God, and now he is in a cell and unsure. Luke writes it down without cleaning it up. If John is permitted to ask, so is everyone else. The answer stitches Isaiah 35 to Isaiah 61 - the blind see, the lame walk, the dead are raised, the poor have good news preached to them. But Isaiah 61 also promises liberty to the captives, and the man asking is a captive, and that line does not come back to him. Which is why the next sentence is: blessed is he who finds no occasion for stumbling in me. John does not get out. He is beheaded in the next chapter's backstory, and he is called the greatest born of women anyway.

At the dinner, a woman comes in with an alabaster jar. She is not Mary Magdalene; that identification was made by a preacher centuries later and there is nothing in the text to support it. Luke does not name her. She weeps on His feet and lets down her hair to dry them, which in that culture was scandalous, and she does it anyway. Simon thinks - he does not say it - that a prophet would know what sort of woman this is, and the thought is answered with a parable about two debtors. Then the question that should stop every reader: Simon, do you see this woman? He has been looking at her all evening and has not seen her once. What follows is a list of things Simon did not do - no water, no kiss, no oil - none of them extravagant, all of them ordinary hospitality, and all three skipped. She has been supplying every one of them with what she had, on the floor, for an hour. And the last word to her is not that she loved well, but that her faith has saved her.

verses.49: Those who sat at the table with him began to say to themselves, “Who is this who even forgives sins?”
verses.50: He said to the woman, “Your faith has saved you. Go in peace.”

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 8 - Women Who Paid For It, Four Kinds of Ground, and a Man in His Right Mind
chapters.title: Women Who Paid For It, Four Kinds of Ground, and a Man in His Right Mind
keyNotes: Verses 1 to 3 are among the most skipped lines in Luke: named women travelling with the group and funding it out of their own money (Luke 8:1-3).
"Who served them from their possessions" makes the financial base of the ministry female. No other Gospel says this (Luke 8:3).
Joanna's husband managed Herod's household. Luke has a named source inside the court that executed John, which may be exactly how he knows what Herod said to himself (Luke 8:3, 9:9).

Mary Magdalene is described as having had seven demons and nothing else. There is not one word anywhere in Scripture about prostitution. That identification comes from a sixth-century sermon (Luke 8:2).
Luke's sower is shorter than Mark's and drops the thirty and sixtyfold. Only a hundred remains (Luke 8:8, Mark 4:8).
"Seeing they may not see" quotes Isaiah 6:9, the words given to Isaiah at his commissioning - a prophet sent to people who would not listen (Luke 8:10, Isaiah 6:9-10).
Only Luke says the seed on the rock lacked moisture, and only Luke says the fall happens "in time of temptation" rather than persecution (Luke 8:6, 13).
Luke's thorns are cares, riches, and pleasures. He adds pleasures to Mark's list, which is consistent with everything else he chooses to record (Luke 8:14, Mark 4:19).
"Hold it tightly, and produce fruit with perseverance" - hypomone, endurance under load. Luke's good soil is measured over time rather than at harvest (Luke 8:15).
"Be careful therefore how you hear." Luke turns the lamp saying into a warning about listening (Luke 8:18).
The family scene is markedly gentler here. Mark has the relatives saying He is out of His mind; Luke keeps only the redefinition, with no rebuke attached (Luke 8:19-21, Mark 3:21).
"Master, master" translates epistates, a word for a person in charge that only Luke uses in the whole New Testament (Luke 8:24).
"Where is your faith?" is softer than Mark's "have you still no faith?" - the same scene, recorded with a different edge (Luke 8:25, Mark 4:40).
Only Luke has the demons begging not to be sent into the abyss, which is the word Revelation uses for the pit (Luke 8:31).
"Sitting at Jesus' feet, clothed and in his right mind" is disciple posture. Mary of Bethany will sit in the same place two chapters later (Luke 8:35, 10:39).
The whole region asks Him to leave, and He goes. He does not argue, and He does not stay where He is not wanted (Luke 8:37).
The one man who asks to come along is the one told to stay. He is sent home to the people who watched him live in a graveyard (Luke 8:38-39).
Two twelves sit side by side: a girl who has been alive twelve years, and a woman who has been bleeding for twelve. One story is interrupted by the other (Luke 8:42-43).

Luke says the woman "had spent all her living on physicians." Mark says the doctors made her worse. Luke, who was one, is noticeably kinder to the profession - and some manuscripts omit his clause altogether (Luke 8:43, Mark 5:26).
She reaches for the fringe of His cloak - the tzitzit that Torah commands on the corners of a garment (Luke 8:44, Numbers 15:38-39).
"I perceived that power has gone out of me" makes the healing something that cost Him (Luke 8:46).
"Daughter" is the only time in the Gospels He addresses a woman that way, and He says it to someone who has been ritually untouchable for twelve years (Luke 8:48).
"She isn't dead, but sleeping" gets Him laughed at, and Luke keeps the ridicule in (Luke 8:52-53).
"He commanded that something be given to her to eat" survives in every account. Resurrection, and then breakfast (Luke 8:55).

intro: Three verses at the head of this chapter are read straight past by almost everybody. He is going through the towns preaching, and with Him are the twelve - and certain women, whom Luke names. Mary called Magdalene. Joanna, the wife of Herod's steward. Susanna. And many others. And then: who served them from their possessions. The ministry was funded by women out of their own money, and no other Gospel says so. Luke reports it in his third sentence as though it were obvious.

Joanna is worth a moment. Her husband ran Herod's household - the same Herod who beheaded John. There is a woman from inside that court out on the road paying for this, which may well be how Luke knows what Herod said to himself in the next chapter. And on Mary Magdalene the text says seven demons and nothing else. There is not a word anywhere in Scripture about her being a prostitute; that was attached to her by a pope preaching in the year 591, and it should not be repeated.

Luke's sower is leaner than Mark's - the thirtyfold and sixtyfold are gone and only the hundred remains - but two things are added. The rock has no moisture. And the fall happens in a time of temptation rather than persecution, which is Mark's word. Temptation is quieter, and it does not look like an attack. His thorns are cares, riches and pleasures, and pleasures is his own addition. Nothing on that list is a sin, which is precisely what makes it dangerous. And his good ground holds the word with perseverance - hypomone, staying under a weight without moving. Luke's harvest is not measured in one season but in how long a person keeps going.

In the storm they wake Him with the word epistates, which appears nowhere in the New Testament outside this Gospel and means the one in charge. Even panicking, that is the word they reach for. And the question afterwards is gentler than Mark's. Mark has have you still no faith. Luke has where is your faith - a real question rather than an accusation.

On the other side of the lake a man with no clothes and no house, driven into the desert by what is in him, ends the scene sitting at Jesus' feet, clothed and in his right mind. At His feet is the posture of a student, and Mary of Bethany will occupy it two chapters later. The town asks Him to leave and He goes, without argument or campaign. And the one man who wants to come is the one told no - go home, and tell what God has done for you. Sometimes the call is to get into the boat, and sometimes it is to go back to the town where everybody watched you at your worst and live there.

The last two stories are folded into each other, and the number twelve is in both. Jairus has a daughter of about twelve, dying; a woman has been bleeding for twelve years. For as long as that girl has been alive, this woman has been unclean, unable to worship normally, unable to be touched. She reaches for the fringe of His cloak - the tzitzit that Torah commands on the corner of a garment, the most Jewish thing on Him. And He stops everything to find her, in a crowd, with a dying child waiting, because she was about to slip away healed and still anonymous, and He will not let her leave without a name. Daughter is the only time in the Gospels He calls a woman that. And the delay caused by stopping for her is the thing that turns a healing into a resurrection.

verses.1: Soon afterwards, he went about through cities and villages, preaching and bringing the good news of God’s Kingdom. With him were the twelve,
verses.2: and certain women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary who was called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out;
verses.3: and Joanna, the wife of Chuzas, Herod’s steward; Susanna; and many others; who served them from their possessions.
verses.4: When a great multitude came together, and people from every city were coming to him, he spoke by a parable.

verses.6: Other seed fell on the rock, and as soon as it grew, it withered away, because it had no moisture.
verses.7: Other fell amid the thorns, and the thorns grew with it, and choked it.

verses.24: They came to him, and awoke him, saying, “Master, master, we are dying!” He awoke, and rebuked the wind and the raging of the water, and they ceased, and it was calm.
