chapters.heading: CHAPTER 9 - Twelve Sent Out Empty-Handed, and a Face Set Toward Jerusalem
chapters.title: Twelve Sent Out Empty-Handed, and a Face Set Toward Jerusalem
keyNotes: They are given both power and authority - dunamis and exousia. The ability to do it and the right to do it are handed over together (Luke 9:1).
Luke's packing list is the barest of the three accounts. No staff, no bag, no bread, no money, no second coat (Luke 9:3, Mark 6:8).
Herod's question - "who is this?" - is the question of the whole chapter, and it is asked first by the man who beheaded John (Luke 9:9).
The feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle that appears in all four Gospels (Luke 9:10-17).
"You give them something to eat" comes before any solution is offered. The impossible instruction is the point (Luke 9:13).
Twelve baskets left over, twelve disciples. Each man who said it could not be done carries away more than they began with (Luke 9:17).
"As he was praying alone" - only Luke puts the great confession immediately after prayer (Luke 9:18).
Peter says "the Christ of God." Luke has neither Matthew's commendation nor Mark's "get behind me, Satan." He records the confession and moves straight to the cross (Luke 9:20, Matthew 16:16-23).
"The Son of Man must suffer" - dei again, the same necessity verb as in chapter 4 (Luke 9:22, 4:43).
"Take up his cross daily." Only Luke has daily, and it changes the saying from a single decision into a repeated one (Luke 9:23, Mark 8:34).
The transfiguration happens while He is praying, and only Luke says so (Luke 9:29).
"His departure" is literally his exodos - the Exodus word. Moses is standing right there while they discuss it (Luke 9:31).
Only Luke tells us what Moses and Elijah were talking about (Luke 9:31).
"Heavy with sleep" - the same three men will sleep again in Gethsemane. Luke sets up the echo (Luke 9:32, 22:45).
"Not knowing what he said" is Luke's own kindness toward Peter, inserted as an explanation (Luke 9:33).
The cloud overshadows them, using the same verb as Gabriel's word to Mary and the cloud on the tabernacle (Luke 9:34, 1:35, Exodus 40:35).
The voice adds something the baptism did not: listen to him. That is the language of Deuteronomy 18 and the prophet like Moses (Luke 9:35, Deuteronomy 18:15).
The boy at the foot of the mountain is "my only child" - Luke's third only child in three chapters, after the widow's son and Jairus's daughter (Luke 9:38, 7:12, 8:42).
"It was concealed from them" is passive. Luke says the failure to understand was itself given, which is a harder statement than simple slowness (Luke 9:45).
The argument about greatness follows the passion prediction immediately, exactly as in Mark. The pattern is consistent and unflattering (Luke 9:46).

"He who is not against us is for us" here, and "he who is not with me is against me" in chapter 11. Both are in Luke. One is about who may serve; the other is about where you stand (Luke 9:50, 11:23).
**Verse 51 is the hinge of the whole Gospel.** "He intently set his face to go to Jerusalem." Ten chapters of travel start here, and almost everything unique to Luke happens on that road (Luke 9:51).
The Samaritans refuse Him for precisely that reason - His face is set toward Jerusalem, and they worshipped at Gerizim (Luke 9:53).
James and John propose calling fire down, citing Elijah. They have just watched Elijah on a mountain discussing an exodus, and they take the wrong lesson (Luke 9:54, 2 Kings 1:10).

Verses 55-56 carry a longer reading that many manuscripts do not have. The WEB prints it; the front matter of the combined edition sets out the evidence, and this book takes no position (Luke 9:55-56).
Three would-be followers get three answers: no home, no funeral, no goodbye. Luke has all three; Matthew has two (Luke 9:57-62, Matthew 8:19-22).
"Leave the dead to bury their own dead" is the hardest sentence in Luke. Burying a father was a sacred obligation, and it is not softened (Luke 9:60).

The last man asks only to say goodbye at home. Elisha asked Elijah for exactly that and was granted it. This man is not, and the difference is the whole point about what has changed (Luke 9:61-62, 1 Kings 19:19-21).

intro: This chapter has a hinge in it. Everything before verse 51 belongs to one book and everything after it to another.

It opens with the twelve being sent out, and what they are given is two words: dunamis, the ability, and exousia, the right to use it. Then the packing list, which is really a list of prohibitions - no staff, no bag, no bread, no money, not even a change of clothes. Which means that every night somebody has to take them in or they sleep outside. The mission is designed so that they cannot be self-sufficient.

Herod asks the question the whole chapter turns on: John I beheaded, but who is this? It is asked by Herod, asked again by Yahshua Himself a dozen verses later, and answered out of a cloud before the chapter ends. Between those, five thousand men and five loaves - the only miracle all four Gospels record. The disciples have already worked out the sensible answer, which is to send everyone away, and they are given an impossible order before any means of obeying it exists. Twelve baskets are left over, one for each man who said it could not be done.

Only Luke tells us He was praying alone before He asked who they say He is, and only Luke says the appearance of His face was altered while He prayed on the mountain. In this Gospel the glory keeps arriving in the middle of prayer. On the mountain, Moses and Elijah discuss - and again only Luke records the subject - His departure, which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem. The Greek word for departure is exodos. They are discussing an exodus, and Moses is standing there while they do it.

The voice from the cloud adds two words it did not use at the Jordan. At the river it was you are my beloved Son. Here it is listen to him, which is Deuteronomy 18 and the prophet like Moses. Then down the mountain into failure, a father with an only son - the third only child in three chapters - and disciples who can do nothing. Another passion prediction follows, and the response to it is an argument about which of them is the greatest. That sequence occurs three times in the Gospels and it never becomes less painful.

Then verse 51: when the days were near that He should be taken up, He set His face to go to Jerusalem. Everything to this point has been Galilee. From here to chapter 19 it is one road, going one place, and He never turns around. Almost everything readers love in this Gospel and find nowhere else - the Samaritan on the Jericho road, the prodigal son, Zacchaeus - happens on it. And the first thing that happens after His face is set is that a Samaritan village refuses Him precisely because of where His face is set. James and John, who thirty verses earlier watched Elijah on a mountain, propose calling down fire. They saw Elijah discussing a rescue and came away thinking about artillery. The full reply in verses 55 and 56 is missing from many manuscripts; the WEB prints it, and whether or not it was original, whoever wrote it understood this Gospel.

verses.1: He called the twelve together, and gave them power and authority over all demons, and to cure diseases.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 10 - Seventy Sent Ahead, a Samaritan on the Jericho Road, and One Thing Needed
chapters.title: Seventy Sent Ahead, a Samaritan on the Jericho Road, and One Thing Needed
keyNotes: Seventy or seventy-two? The manuscripts are split almost evenly, and the WEB prints seventy. Genesis 10 lists the nations of the world - seventy in the Hebrew, seventy-two in the Greek - so either number is a quiet claim about the whole earth (Luke 10:1, 17).
They are sent "ahead of him into every city where he was about to come." This is an advance party for a journey already under way, not a substitute for Him (Luke 10:1).
They are told to pray for labourers, and then immediately sent. They become the answer to the prayer they were told to pray (Luke 10:2-3).
"Greet no one on the way" is not rudeness. Eastern greetings were long and obligating, and the instruction is about urgency (Luke 10:4).
"A son of peace" is a Hebrew idiom - a person characterised by peace - rather than a title (Luke 10:6).

"Eat the things that are set before you" is said to Jewish messengers entering houses whose kitchens they cannot vouch for. Paul gives the same instruction almost word for word (Luke 10:8, 1 Corinthians 10:27).
Chorazin is named in the whole Bible only here and in the parallel in Matthew. We know almost nothing about it, and it was under a woe (Luke 10:13).
The comparison is deliberately humiliating: Tyre, Sidon and Sodom - the standard bywords for pagan wickedness - would have repented (Luke 10:13-14).

"I saw Satan having fallen like lightning from heaven." The Greek leaves the timing open, and readers have placed it before creation, at the cross, and right there in the seventy's mission. This book does not settle it (Luke 10:18).
"Authority to tread on serpents and scorpions" is a promise of protection in the work, not an instruction to go and find snakes. People have died reading it the other way (Luke 10:19).
"Don't rejoice in this... but rejoice that your names are written in heaven" corrects a joy that was not wrong, only smaller than the one available (Luke 10:20).
"Jesus rejoiced in the Holy Spirit" is the only place in the Gospels He is described as rejoicing (Luke 10:21).
The lawyer stands up to test Him and is handed the question back. He then answers it correctly himself, joining Deuteronomy 6:5 to Leviticus 19:18 (Luke 10:26-27).
"Desiring to justify himself" tells you what the second question is for. The parable answers self-justification, not ignorance (Luke 10:29).
Jerusalem down to Jericho is seventeen miles and a drop of well over three thousand feet, through country notorious for robbery. "Going down" is literal (Luke 10:30).

Both the priest and the Levite are going down - away from Jerusalem - so their temple duty was most likely already behind them. The corpse-uncleanness excuse is the kindest reading available, and it still does not work (Luke 10:31-32).
The hero is a Samaritan, told to a Jewish lawyer. The shock is not that he helps; it is that he is the one who turns out to have kept the law the lawyer just quoted (Luke 10:33).
Oil and wine were the ordinary first aid of the period - and also the elements of temple offering. The Samaritan pours out on the road what the priest handled in the sanctuary (Luke 10:34).
Two denarii is about two days' wages, which would cover a couple of weeks at an inn - and he leaves an open account on top of it (Luke 10:35).
The question comes back inverted. Not "who is my neighbour?" but "which of these three became a neighbour?" Neighbour stops being a category to be checked and becomes something you do (Luke 10:36).
The lawyer cannot bring himself to say the word Samaritan. He says "he who showed mercy on him" (Luke 10:37).
"Sat at Jesus' feet" is the technical description of a rabbinic student. Paul uses it of his own training under Gamaliel (Luke 10:39, Acts 22:3).
"Distracted" is perispao - pulled in several directions at once. Martha is not lazy; she is fragmented (Luke 10:40).
"Martha, Martha" - the doubled name is used elsewhere in this Gospel for Simon and later for Saul. It is affection, not a telling-off (Luke 10:41, 22:31).
"One thing is needed" is the WEB's reading; some manuscripts have "few things are needed, or one." The point survives either way (Luke 10:42).

intro: From here to chapter 19 the setting is a road, and most of what happens on it is found in no other Gospel. This chapter is where that begins to pay.

Seventy men are sent out two by two, ahead of Him, into every town He is about to enter. Some Bibles read seventy-two, and the manuscripts are genuinely split; either way the number points at the same thing, because Genesis 10 lists the nations of the world and, depending on which text is read, there are seventy of them or seventy-two. It is a number about the whole earth. And verse 2 sits next to verse 3 for a reason: pray the Lord of the harvest to send out labourers, and then, go your ways, I send you out. They become the answer to the prayer they were told to pray.

They come back electric - even the demons are subject to us - and the joy is not squashed. Something larger is said, and then the joy is gently redirected: do not rejoice that the spirits submit, but that your names are written in heaven. The work going well is a real joy, and it is not the one that will hold a person when it stops going well.

The lawyer's exchange is a set piece worth watching move by move. He stands up to test Him, and the question is handed back. He answers it himself, correctly, stitching Deuteronomy 6 to Leviticus 19 without hesitating, and is told to do this and live. That should end it. But the text says exactly what happens next and why: desiring to justify himself, he asked, and who is my neighbour? That is not a request for information. That is a man looking for a boundary, asking where the obligation stops.

So, the Jericho road - seventeen miles downhill, three thousand feet of descent, through country notorious for robbery. A man is stripped, beaten and left half dead, which matters, because from a distance nobody can tell whether he is alive or a corpse. A priest crosses over. A Levite does the same. The usual defence is ritual purity, but both men are going down, away from Jerusalem, with their duty behind them rather than ahead. That is the most generous reading available and it still does not hold.

Then a Samaritan - not a foreigner but a heretic, a neighbour with the wrong temple on the wrong mountain and centuries of bad blood. He uses oil and wine, the ordinary first aid of the period and also the elements of temple offering, so that what the priest handled in the sanctuary is poured out on the road. He puts the man on his own animal, which means he is now walking, and he leaves an open account at the inn. And the closing question is inverted. Not which of these three was the neighbour I was obliged to help, but which of them became a neighbour to the man in the ditch. The lawyer wanted a category and was handed a verb - and he cannot bring himself to say the word Samaritan, only he who showed mercy. The house at Bethany teaches the same lesson from the other side, and it is usually misread. Mary is sitting where a student sits; Paul says he was brought up at the feet of Gamaliel, and in that world the seat was not offered to a woman. Martha is not the villain - she is doing the hospitality the Samaritan was just praised for. But the word is perispao, pulled apart in several directions, and when she finally speaks it comes out as Lord, do you not care. The service has curdled into resentment and the resentment has turned on Him.

verses.1: Now after these things, the Lord also appointed seventy others, and sent them two by two ahead of him into every city and place, where he was about to come.
verses.2: Then he said to them, “The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the laborers are few. Pray therefore to the Lord of the harvest, that he may send out laborers into his harvest.
verses.3: Go your ways. Behold, I send you out as lambs among wolves.
verses.4: Carry no purse, nor wallet, nor sandals. Greet no one on the way.
verses.5: Into whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace be to this house.’
verses.6: If a son of peace is there, your peace will rest on him; but if not, it will return to you.
verses.7: Remain in that same house, eating and drinking the things they give, for the laborer is worthy of his wages. Don’t go from house to house.
verses.8: Into whatever city you enter, and they receive you, eat the things that are set before you.
verses.9: Heal the sick who are therein, and tell them, ‘God’s Kingdom has come near to you.’
verses.10: But into whatever city you enter, and they don’t receive you, go out into its streets and say,
verses.11: ‘Even the dust from your city that clings to us, we wipe off against you. Nevertheless know this, that God’s Kingdom has come near to you.’
verses.12: I tell you, it will be more tolerable in that day for Sodom than for that city.
verses.13: “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works had been done in Tyre and Sidon which were done in you, they would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes.
verses.14: But it will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon in the judgment than for you.
verses.15: You, Capernaum, who are exalted to heaven, will be brought down to Hades.
verses.16: Whoever listens to you listens to me, and whoever rejects you rejects me. Whoever rejects me rejects him who sent me.”
verses.17: The seventy returned with joy, saying, “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name!”
verses.18: He said to them, “I saw Satan having fallen like lightning from heaven.
verses.19: Behold, I give you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy. Nothing will in any way hurt you.
verses.20: Nevertheless, don’t rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.”
verses.21: In that same hour Jesus rejoiced in the Holy Spirit, and said, “I thank you, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding, and revealed them to little children. Yes, Father, for so it was well-pleasing in your sight.”
verses.22: Turning to the disciples, he said, “All things have been delivered to me by my Father. No one knows who the Son is, except the Father, and who the Father is, except the Son, and he to whomever the Son desires to reveal him.”
verses.23: Turning to the disciples, he said privately, “Blessed are the eyes which see the things that you see,
verses.24: for I tell you that many prophets and kings desired to see the things which you see, and didn’t see them, and to hear the things which you hear, and didn’t hear them.”
verses.25: Behold, a certain lawyer stood up and tested him, saying, “Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?”
verses.26: He said to him, “What is written in the law? How do you read it?”
verses.27: He answered, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your strength, and with all your mind; and your neighbor as yourself.”
verses.28: He said to him, “You have answered correctly. Do this, and you will live.”
verses.29: But he, desiring to justify himself, asked Jesus, “Who is my neighbor?”
verses.30: Jesus answered, “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers, who both stripped him and beat him, and departed, leaving him half dead.
verses.31: By chance a certain priest was going down that way. When he saw him, he passed by on the other side.
verses.32: In the same way a Levite also, when he came to the place, and saw him, passed by on the other side.
verses.33: But a certain Samaritan, as he traveled, came where he was. When he saw him, he was moved with compassion,
verses.34: came to him, and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. He set him on his own animal, and brought him to an inn, and took care of him.
verses.35: On the next day, when he departed, he took out two denarii, and gave them to the host, and said to him, ‘Take care of him. Whatever you spend beyond that, I will repay you when I return.’
verses.36: Now which of these three do you think seemed to be a neighbor to him who fell among the robbers?”
verses.37: He said, “He who showed mercy on him.” Then Jesus said to him, “Go and do likewise.”
verses.38: As they went on their way, he entered into a certain village, and a certain woman named Martha received him into her house.
verses.39: She had a sister called Mary, who also sat at Jesus’ feet, and heard his word.
verses.40: But Martha was distracted with much serving, and she came up to him, and said, “Lord, don’t you care that my sister left me to serve alone? Ask her therefore to help me.”
verses.41: Jesus answered her, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things,
verses.42: but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.”

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 11 - Teach Us to Pray, a Finger of God, and Woes at Dinner
chapters.title: Teach Us to Pray, a Finger of God, and Woes at Dinner
keyNotes: They ask after watching Him pray, not after a lesson on prayer. The request comes out of observing something they wanted (Luke 11:1).

Luke's prayer is shorter than Matthew's, and a good many manuscripts of Luke are shorter still. The WEB prints the fuller form; the differences are worth knowing about and change nothing essential (Luke 11:2-4, Matthew 6:9-13).

"Daily" translates epiousios, a word that appears nowhere in Greek literature outside this prayer. Its meaning is genuinely uncertain - for today, for tomorrow, or necessary for existence (Luke 11:3).
Luke has "forgive us our sins"; Matthew has "debts." The second half - everyone who is indebted to us - keeps the financial image in both (Luke 11:4, Matthew 6:12).

The friend at midnight turns on anaideia, translated here as persistence but more literally shamelessness. It may describe the asker's nerve, or the householder's unwillingness to be shamed. Both readings are ancient (Luke 11:8).
"Keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking" are continuous-action imperatives. One request is not what is being described (Luke 11:9).
Matthew's version ends with the Father giving "good gifts." Luke ends it with the Holy Spirit. In this Gospel the answer to prayer is finally a Person (Luke 11:13, Matthew 7:11).

Beelzebul goes back to Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron whom Ahaziah consulted. The name means something like lord of the height, or lord of the flies, depending on the spelling (Luke 11:15, 2 Kings 1:2).
"By God's finger" where Matthew has "the Spirit of God." The finger of God is what Pharaoh's magicians said when they hit the limit of what they could reproduce (Luke 11:20, Exodus 8:19).
The strong man is disarmed rather than negotiated with, and the armour he trusted is taken (Luke 11:21-22).
"He that is not with me is against me" sits two chapters from "he who is not against us is for us." One is about who may work; this one is about where you stand (Luke 11:23, 9:50).
The swept and ordered house is worse off than the dirty one. An emptied life that stays empty is not a safe life (Luke 11:24-26).
The woman blesses His mother; He redirects the blessing to whoever hears and keeps the word. He has already done this once, to His actual family (Luke 11:27-28, 8:21).
Luke's sign of Jonah is not three days in a fish - that is Matthew. Here the sign is Jonah himself, a preacher arriving from somewhere else and being believed (Luke 11:30, Matthew 12:40).
The Queen of the South and the men of Nineveh are both Gentiles, called as witnesses against the generation standing in front of Him (Luke 11:31-32).
A "good eye" in Hebrew idiom means generous and a "bad eye" means stingy - which is why the lamp saying lands nine verses later on giving to the needy (Luke 11:34, 41).
He does not wash before the meal, and He clearly does not do it by accident. The whole confrontation follows from a deliberate omission (Luke 11:38).
Luke's version of cleaning the inside of the cup is almsgiving. Give what is within, and everything is clean (Luke 11:41).
"You tithe mint and rue" - and He does not tell them to stop. "You ought to have done these, and not to have left the other undone" (Luke 11:42).

"Hidden graves" is a sharper insult than it sounds. Walking over an unmarked grave made a person unclean without their knowing it - so the accusation is that they defile people who cannot tell it is happening (Luke 11:44, Numbers 19:16).
The lawyers load burdens and will not lift a finger - and the last thing described as a finger in this chapter was God's, casting out demons (Luke 11:46, 20).
"From the blood of Abel to the blood of Zachariah" spans the whole Hebrew canon: Genesis is first, and in the Hebrew ordering Chronicles is last (Luke 11:51, Genesis 4:8, 2 Chronicles 24:20-21).
"You took away the key of knowledge" - not lost, took away. And then stood in the doorway (Luke 11:52).

intro: Lord, teach us to pray. And notice what prompts it: He had finished praying in a certain place. They are not asking because prayer came up in a sermon; they are asking because they watched Him do it and wanted whatever that was.

What He gives them is short - shorter than the version most people learned, and in many manuscripts of Luke shorter still. The texts do not all agree here and the WEB prints the fuller form; nothing essential moves either way. But the shape is the thing. Father. Your name. Your kingdom. Your will. Then our bread, our forgiveness, our protection. God first and then us, with the bread taken one day at a time, like manna, which could not be stockpiled.

The story that follows is not polite. A man bangs on a friend's door at midnight because guests have arrived and he has nothing to feed them, and the friend inside tells him to go away. The word for what finally gets the man up is anaideia, which means shamelessness rather than persistence. So the lesson is not that God is reluctant and must be worn down. It is that the man outside is not embarrassed to ask. And the imperatives are continuous - keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking - not knock once.

Then the punchline, and Luke's differs from Matthew's in a way that matters. Matthew says the Father will give good gifts to those who ask. Luke says He will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him. The best thing on the table is not a thing.

The Beelzebul accusation is answered with straightforward logic - a kingdom at war with itself falls - and then with a phrase easy to miss. Matthew says the Spirit of God; Luke says the finger of God, which comes out of Exodus, where it is what Pharaoh's magicians said when they finally struck something they could not duplicate. The claim is that the plagues are happening again and the accusers are standing on the wrong side of them. And the warning that follows is genuinely unsettling: a spirit goes out, wanders, returns and finds the house swept and in order, empty and available, and moves back in with seven others. Being cleaned out is not the finish line. An empty house is not a safe house.

When a woman blesses His mother, He turns it - blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it. He had already done that in chapter 8 with His family standing outside; twice now He has declined to make His bloodline the point. Then the dinner, where He does not perform the ritual hand-washing and His host is astonished. This is not hygiene and it is not Torah but tradition, and He knew exactly what He was doing. What follows is everything wrong with the room said out loud. He does not tell them to stop tithing herbs; He says these ought to have been done without leaving the other undone. The problem is not the mint, it is the justice. And the unmarked graves are a vicious image, because walking over a grave defiled a person without his knowledge - people are being contaminated by these men and cannot tell. When a lawyer objects that this insults his profession too, the answer is yes, and here is yours: you load people with burdens and will not lift a finger to help. The last finger in this chapter belonged to God, and it was casting out demons.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 12 - Yeast, Sparrows, Barns, and a Master Who Serves
chapters.title: Yeast, Sparrows, Barns, and a Master Who Serves
keyNotes: A crowd of thousands is trampling each other, and He turns to speak to the disciples first. The size of the crowd is the reason for the warning that follows (Luke 12:1).
Hypocrisy is named as yeast - small, invisible, and it changes the whole loaf. The word hypokrites is a stage actor (Luke 12:1).
"Nothing covered up that will not be revealed" is the reason hypocrisy is pointless rather than merely wrong. It has a shelf life (Luke 12:2-3).
"Don't be afraid... but I will warn you whom you should fear." This is the only fear commanded in the passage, and it is aimed away from the people who can kill you (Luke 12:4-5).
Gehenna is a real place - the Valley of Hinnom, immediately outside Jerusalem, with a history of child sacrifice under Ahaz and Manasseh (Luke 12:5, Jeremiah 7:31).
Matthew prices sparrows at two for one coin; Luke says five for two. Buy in bulk and the fifth one is thrown in free - and God has not forgotten that one either (Luke 12:6, Matthew 10:29).
The saying about blaspheming the Spirit sits here in a context of denial under pressure, which is worth noticing before anyone applies it to themselves (Luke 12:8-10).
The man who wants his inheritance divided receives no ruling whatsoever. He came for arbitration and got a diagnosis (Luke 12:13-15).
The rich fool says I or my eleven times in four verses, and the only person he consults is himself. His soul is his conversation partner right up to the moment it is required of him (Luke 12:17-19).
"Your soul is required of you" uses a verb for demanding back what was lent. The life was never his to bank (Luke 12:20).
Nothing in the parable says he cheated anybody. His land simply produced well. That is what makes it frightening (Luke 12:16).
"Consider the ravens" - not birds in general. Ravens are unclean, and they are the specific birds Psalm 147 says God feeds (Luke 12:24, Psalm 147:9).
Matthew has lilies and birds; Luke chooses the unclean bird and keeps the lily. The pattern is consistent with everything else he selects (Luke 12:24, 27, Matthew 6:26).
"Little flock" appears nowhere else in Scripture, and it is said to a group that has just been told not to be anxious about food (Luke 12:32).
"Sell that which you have, and give gifts to the needy" is stated without hedging. Luke has said versions of this in every chapter of this volume (Luke 12:33, 11:41).
"Let your waist be dressed" is literally let your loins be girded - the posture of Passover night, dressed to travel at a moment's notice (Luke 12:35, Exodus 12:11).
Verse 37 is the most startling image in the chapter: the master comes home, finds them awake, and puts on an apron and serves them. That inversion is the Gospel in one sentence (Luke 12:37).
Peter asks whether the parable is for them or for everybody, and gets an answer about stewards - which is to say, yes, and especially for you (Luke 12:41-42).
"To whomever much is given, of him will much be required" is spoken to the people with the most access, not the least (Luke 12:48).
"I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how distressed I am until it is accomplished" - the baptism is the cross, and He says He is under pressure until it happens (Luke 12:50).
"Not peace but division" is quoted almost directly from Micah 7:6, where the household collapse is a symptom of a nation in trouble (Luke 12:51-53, Micah 7:6).
They can read a westerly cloud and a south wind and cannot read the moment they are standing in. The failure is not intelligence (Luke 12:54-56).
The last paragraph is about settling out of court on the way, and it is a parable about urgency, not a lesson in litigation (Luke 12:58-59).

intro: Thousands are trampling each other to get near Him, and with a crowd that size in front of Him the first thing He does is turn to the twelve and warn them about yeast.

Yeast is chosen for what it does - a tiny amount, invisible once it is in, changing the whole loaf. Nobody decides to become a hypocrite; it works through. And the word itself means a stage actor, someone playing to a room, which is exactly the temptation when thousands are watching. Then the reason it is finally pointless: there is nothing covered that will not be revealed, and what was said in the dark gets heard in daylight. Pretending is not only wrong; it has an expiry date.

The teaching on fear is put with great care. Do not be afraid of those who kill the body and can do nothing more - but I will warn you whom you should fear. This is not a passage about being frightened of God in general. It is about which fear governs when two of them compete, and the people who can kill you are not the ones.

And then, immediately, sparrows. Five for two coins - Matthew has two for one coin, which means the fifth was thrown in free, the one nobody was paying for - and not one of them is forgotten by God. The hairs of the head are numbered. The hardest thing to fear and the gentlest reason not to be afraid arrive back to back, in the same breath.

A man shouts out of the crowd asking for a ruling on his inheritance, and no ruling is given. He does not take the case; He goes after what is underneath it. And then the rich fool, where the striking thing is what is absent. He did not steal or defraud anyone. The ground produced abundantly - he had a good year, and that is all. Count the pronouns: my crops, my barns, my grain, my goods, my soul, eleven first-person words in four verses. And the only person he speaks to in the entire parable is himself. God interrupts a man mid-conversation with his own soul, and the word for required is the word for calling in a loan. The life he had been budgeting was never his capital.

From that He turns to the disciples and says therefore do not be anxious, which is a strange therefore until it comes into focus. The rich man's problem and the anxious man's problem are the same problem approached from opposite ends; both are trying to secure a life by managing supply. Consider the ravens - not birds in general, ravens, which are unclean, and which Psalm 147 says God feeds when they cry. The God who feeds the bird nobody would keep is not going to overlook a person. Then little flock, a phrase that occurs once in Scripture, said to a small and anxious group with no money, and finished with it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the Kingdom. Not to sell it, not to make them earn it. And the chapter's last picture is a master who comes home, finds his servants awake, dresses himself for service, sits them down and serves them - which no household in that world worked like, and which happens in chapter 22, in an upper room, with a towel.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 13 - Blood in the Sacrifices, One More Year for the Fig Tree, and a Hen Over Jerusalem
chapters.title: Blood in the Sacrifices, One More Year for the Fig Tree, and a Hen Over Jerusalem
keyNotes: The massacre in verse 1 is recorded nowhere else - not in Josephus, not anywhere. It fits what we know of Pilate's temper, and that is all we can honestly say about it (Luke 13:1).
Nobody asked Him a question. They brought Him a story, and He answered the assumption inside it: that catastrophe measures guilt (Luke 13:2).

He refuses the arithmetic twice, and both times He replaces it with the same sentence - unless you repent, you will all perish in the same way. He will not let anyone stand outside a tragedy and grade it (Luke 13:3, 5).
The tower in Siloam is equally unknown to history. Eighteen people died in an accident, and He treats accident and atrocity exactly the same way (Luke 13:4).

"You will all perish in the same way" landed inside forty years. When Jerusalem fell, blood did run in the temple courts and walls did come down on people. He is not scoring a point; He is trying to get a city off a road it is already walking (Luke 13:5).

A fig tree planted in a vineyard is an odd but real arrangement - fruit trees were grown among the vines. The complaint is not only that it is barren but that it is drinking what the vines need (Luke 13:6-7).
"Why does it waste the soil?" - the verb is katargeo, to render useless. The tree is not neutral. It is costing something (Luke 13:7).

The vinedresser does not argue with the verdict. He asks for time and volunteers the labour: let me dig around it and put manure on it. Grace here is not leniency, it is somebody kneeling in the dirt (Luke 13:8).
And the reprieve has an end date. "If it bears fruit, fine; but if not, after that, you can cut it down" (Luke 13:9).
"A spirit of infirmity eighteen years" - Luke, the physician, gives us both a cause and a clinical description: she was bent together and could not raise herself up at all (Luke 13:11).
She did not ask. She did not cry out. He saw her, and He called her over (Luke 13:12).
"You are freed" is apolelusai - a release word, used of discharging a debt or letting a prisoner go. He uses the same root three verses later about untying an ox (Luke 13:12, 15).
The synagogue ruler is furious with Him and says so to the congregation. He rebukes the crowd for coming, rather than face the man who healed her (Luke 13:14).
"You hypocrites" is plural. The answer goes to the room, not to one official (Luke 13:15).

The argument is made from inside the Sabbath, not against it. They already loosed and watered their animals on that day; He does not overturn their practice, He follows it to its conclusion (Luke 13:15).
"A daughter of Abraham" is a phrase found nowhere else in the Gospels. Bent over in the back of a synagogue for eighteen years, and He says out loud that she is a covenant heir (Luke 13:16).

"Whom Satan had bound" and "be freed from this bondage" - binding and loosing language, on the one day of the week that is about release. The Sabbath is not the obstacle to her healing; it is the argument for it (Luke 13:16).
The adversaries were "disappointed" - kataischuno, put to shame. The crowd rejoiced. Luke keeps showing us the two reactions in the same sentence (Luke 13:17).
Matthew's mustard seed is sown in a field; Luke's is put in a man's own garden. It is a domestic image - the smallest thing you would bother to plant, in the plot behind your house (Luke 13:19).

"The birds of the sky live in its branches" is borrowed language. In Ezekiel and Daniel the great tree with birds nesting in it is a kingdom sheltering the nations - which is exactly what He is claiming for a garden weed (Luke 13:19).

Three measures of flour is roughly enough bread for a hundred people. It is the same quantity Sarah kneaded for the three visitors. The woman is not baking a loaf; she is catering a feast (Luke 13:21).

Yeast has been a warning image two chapters earlier - beware the yeast of the Pharisees. Here it is the Kingdom. The image is not moral, it is mechanical: something small, hidden, and impossible to stop once it is in the dough (Luke 13:21, 12:1).
"Are they few who are saved?" is a speculative question about other people. He answers with a singular imperative aimed at the man asking: strive - agonizomai, the word for a contest (Luke 13:23-24).
The narrow door is not narrow-mindedness. The problem in the parable is not the width of the door but the hour: eventually the master gets up and shuts it (Luke 13:25).

"We ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets" - proximity is not relationship. They are claiming acquaintance, and He says the one thing that cannot be argued with: I don't know where you come from (Luke 13:26-27).
East, west, north and south is the language of the scattered being gathered. The shock is who is inside and who is standing outside watching (Luke 13:28-29).
The Pharisees who warn Him about Herod may be genuinely kind or may be running Herod's errand to move Him along. Luke does not tell us, and the answer is the same either way (Luke 13:31).
"That fox" is the only insult He is ever recorded giving a ruler. A fox is not a lion - it is a small nuisance predator with a reputation for cunning and no real power (Luke 13:32).
"The third day I complete my mission" - the verb is teleioumai, to be finished or brought to its goal. Herod's threat cannot move the timetable by a day (Luke 13:32).
"It can't be that a prophet would perish outside of Jerusalem" is bitter irony, not doctrine. The holy city has become the safest place in the world to kill a prophet (Luke 13:33).
The hen is the only maternal image He ever uses of Himself. Not an eagle, not a lion - a bird with no defence except her own body over the chicks (Luke 13:34).
"How often I wanted... and you refused" is a sentence about a will that has been resisted for centuries. He is not describing one visit (Luke 13:34).
"Your house is left to you desolate" uses Jeremiah's words about the temple - I have forsaken my house. The house is still standing when He says it (Luke 13:35).
The last line is not a threat. It is a date: you will not see me until you say, blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. The exile from His face has a stated end (Luke 13:35).

intro: The chapter begins with somebody bringing news into the room. Pilate has killed a group of Galileans while they were offering sacrifice, and their blood has run into the blood of the animals - murder and desecration in one act. Nobody actually asks a question. They tell the story, and the question underneath it is answered anyway: what did those men do?

That instinct has never gone away. Something terrible happens and the human heart begins looking for the reason the victim had it coming. It is not always cruelty; often it is fear, because finding the reason it happened to them is a way of proving it cannot happen to us. And the arithmetic is refused. Do you think they were worse sinners? I tell you, no. Then a second story nobody brought - a tower in Siloam, eighteen dead in what would now be called an accident - and the same answer. Both times the refusal is followed by the same sentence: unless you repent, you will all perish in the same way. He is not saying suffering is random and meaningless. He is saying the question is being asked about the wrong people, and that the clock is running.

The fig tree is the same message with the anger taken out. Three years the owner has come looking for fruit, and a fig tree in a vineyard is not merely unproductive but expensive, drinking water the vines need. And the vinedresser does not defend the tree or dispute the verdict. He asks for one more year and volunteers to spend it on his knees in the dirt, digging and manuring around something that has given him nothing. Then: if not, after that, you can cut it down. The reprieve is real and it has an end.

The woman bent double for eighteen years is in the synagogue, which is the detail worth stopping on - eighteen years of showing up. She asks for nothing; He sees her, calls her over, and tells her she is freed. The word is a release word, the kind used of a cancelled debt or an opened cell. And the ruler of the synagogue does not confront Him. He turns and scolds the congregation about scheduling, having just watched a woman stand up straight for the first time in eighteen years.

The answer comes back plural, aimed at everyone nodding along, and it is argued from inside the Sabbath rather than against it. Every one of them unties an ox on that day and leads it to water; they already do this, for livestock. Ought not this woman, a daughter of Abraham, bound by Satan for eighteen long years, be loosed on the Sabbath? Loosed - the same word. The Sabbath is not the obstacle to her healing; it is the argument for it. What better day for a bound woman to be set free than the day that exists for release?

Two of the shortest parables follow. A mustard seed planted in a garden becomes a tree with birds nesting in it, which is the image Ezekiel and Daniel use for an empire sheltering the nations. And yeast is hidden in three measures of flour - about fifty pounds, bread for a hundred people, catering rather than dinner. Yeast has been a warning word in this Gospel, but the image here is mechanical rather than moral: something small, hidden, and impossible to remove once it is in the dough. Then a speculative question about how many are being saved, answered with a singular imperative and a picture of a door that will one day be shut, with people outside claiming acquaintance - we ate and drank in your presence. Proximity is not relationship. And the chapter ends not in judgment but in grief: a hen with no defence except her own body over the chicks, a house left desolate while it is still standing, and an until attached to the end of it.

verses.1: Now there were some present at the same time who told him about the Galileans, whose blood Pilate had mixed with their sacrifices.
verses.2: Jesus answered them, “Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered such things?
verses.3: I tell you, no, but unless you repent, you will all perish in the same way.
verses.4: Or those eighteen, on whom the tower in Siloam fell, and killed them; do you think that they were worse offenders than all the men who dwell in Jerusalem?
verses.5: I tell you, no, but, unless you repent, you will all perish in the same way.”
verses.6: He spoke this parable. “A certain man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came seeking fruit on it, and found none.
verses.7: He said to the vine dresser, ‘Behold, these three years I have come looking for fruit on this fig tree, and found none. Cut it down. Why does it waste the soil?’
verses.8: He answered, ‘Lord, leave it alone this year also, until I dig around it, and fertilize it.
verses.9: If it bears fruit, fine; but if not, after that, you can cut it down.’”
verses.10: He was teaching in one of the synagogues on the Sabbath day.
verses.11: Behold, there was a woman who had a spirit of infirmity eighteen years, and she was bent over, and could in no way straighten herself up.
verses.12: When Jesus saw her, he called her, and said to her, “Woman, you are freed from your infirmity.”
verses.13: He laid his hands on her, and immediately she stood up straight, and glorified God.
verses.14: The ruler of the synagogue, being indignant because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, said to the multitude, “There are six days in which men ought to work. Therefore come on those days and be healed, and not on the Sabbath day!”
verses.15: Therefore the Lord answered him, “You hypocrites! Doesn’t each one of you free his ox or his donkey from the stall on the Sabbath, and lead him away to water?
verses.16: Ought not this woman, being a daughter of Abraham, whom Satan had bound eighteen long years, be freed from this bondage on the Sabbath day?”
verses.17: As he said these things, all his adversaries were disappointed, and all the multitude rejoiced for all the glorious things that were done by him.
verses.18: He said, “What is God’s Kingdom like? To what shall I compare it?

verses.21: It is like yeast, which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, until it was all leavened.”
verses.22: He went on his way through cities and villages, teaching, and traveling on to Jerusalem.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 14 - A Watched Table, the Lowest Seat, and the Cost of the Tower
chapters.title: A Watched Table, the Lowest Seat, and the Cost of the Tower
keyNotes: "They were watching him" is parateréo - to watch closely, out of the corner of the eye. The same word is used of lying in wait. He accepts a dinner invitation knowing the room is a trap (Luke 14:1).
The man with dropsy is "in front of him" - placed, not passing through. Whether he was put there or came on his own, everyone in the room can see him (Luke 14:2).

Dropsy is the old name for oedema, and Luke is the only writer in the New Testament to use the medical term. It is a thirst that gets worse the more the body holds - which ancient writers used as a picture of greed, at a dinner table full of it (Luke 14:2).
He asks permission before He heals: is it lawful? They will not answer, because both answers cost them something. Their silence is the admission (Luke 14:3-4).
"He took him, and healed him, and let him go" - the man is released before the argument starts. He does not have to stand there as an exhibit (Luke 14:4).

"If your son or an ox fell into a well" - some manuscripts read donkey rather than son; the WEB prints son. Either way the argument is the same one He used in the synagogue: you already do this (Luke 14:5).
This is the second Sabbath controversy in two chapters, and He answers both from inside the Sabbath rather than against it (Luke 14:5, 13:15).
The "best seats" are the protoklisiai - the couch places nearest the host. Seating at a formal meal was a public ranking, and everyone in the room knew exactly where they had been put (Luke 14:7-8).
The advice is almost word for word out of Proverbs. He is quoting their own wisdom literature back at men who consider themselves its experts (Luke 14:8-10, Proverbs 25:6-7).
Read as etiquette it is shrewd; read as parable it is terrifying. Luke calls it a parable in verse 7, which tells us the host in the story is not the Pharisee (Luke 14:7).
"Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled" is the hinge of the chapter, and He says it again word for word after the Pharisee and the tax collector (Luke 14:11, 18:14).

Then He turns on the host. Do not invite the people who can invite you back. Reciprocal hospitality was the engine of the whole patronage system - He is not tinkering with the guest list, He is unplugging the machine (Luke 14:12).

The four groups He names - poor, maimed, lame, blind - are the same categories excluded from priestly service and, in some communities of the period, from the assembly. He puts them at the head table (Luke 14:13).
"You will be repaid in the resurrection of the righteous" assumes a resurrection sorted into orders, which is Daniel's language. Paul says the same thing standing before Felix (Luke 14:14).
The guest in verse 15 makes a pious noise - blessed is he who will feast in God's Kingdom - and is answered with a parable in which everyone invited to exactly that feast says no (Luke 14:15-16).

Two invitations were the custom: an invitation accepted in advance, then a servant sent when the food was ready. These men had already said yes. The refusals come after the meat is cooked (Luke 14:17).
Every excuse is respectable. A field, five yoke of oxen, a new wife - property, business, family. Nobody says they do not want to come (Luke 14:18-20).

The excuses echo the exemptions Torah grants from military service - a new house, a new vineyard, a new wife. Legitimate ground for missing a war is being used to miss a supper (Luke 14:18-20, Deuteronomy 20:5-7).
Nobody bought a field or five yoke of oxen unseen. The excuses are not only refusals, they are insults dressed as errands (Luke 14:18-19).
The master's anger does not cancel the party. It widens it - first the streets and lanes inside the city, then the highways and hedges outside the walls (Luke 14:21, 23).

"Compel them to come in" is anankazo - insist. In a culture where a poor man would refuse an honour twice out of propriety, the servant has to keep pressing. It has been used to justify force, and the parable will not carry that weight (Luke 14:23).
"There is still room" is the servant's report, and it is the most hopeful line in the chapter (Luke 14:22).
Then He turns to the crowds - the great multitudes going with Him - and starts subtracting. He is not recruiting. He is filtering (Luke 14:25).

"Doesn't disregard his own father" translates the Greek word for hate, and it is a Semitic comparative - Leah is "hated" beside Rachel, Esau beside Jacob. Matthew renders the same saying as loves more than me (Luke 14:26).
"And his own life also" is the clause that stops the idiom from becoming an escape route (Luke 14:26).
"Bear his own cross" was not a metaphor to that crowd. They had watched condemned men carry the crossbeam through their own streets, and nobody carrying one was coming back (Luke 14:27).
The two little parables are not about being cautious. Both men are told to sit down and count - and in both, the point is finishing, not starting (Luke 14:28-32).

The king with ten thousand against twenty thousand is not told how to win. He is told to send an envoy and ask for terms. Sometimes the honest count ends in surrender to the stronger King (Luke 14:31-32).
"Renounce all that he has" is apotassomai - the word for taking leave of somebody at a door. It is not necessarily disposal; it is release of ownership (Luke 14:33).

Salt from the Dead Sea marshes was mixed with gypsum and could genuinely leach until only the useless mineral was left. Flat salt is not merely weak, it is contaminant - fit for neither the soil nor the manure pile (Luke 14:34-35).
"He who has ears to hear, let him hear" is attached to the hardest paragraph in the chapter, not the easiest (Luke 14:35).

intro: He goes out to dinner and the dinner is an ambush. It is a Sabbath, the host is a ruler of the Pharisees, and the text says plainly that they were watching Him - a word used for lying in wait.

In front of Him is a man with dropsy, what would now be called oedema: a body swelling with fluid it cannot shed, and a thirst that worsens the more it holds. Whether the man was invited or placed there, everybody in the room can see what is about to happen. And He asks permission first. Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath? Nobody answers, because neither answer is affordable, and the silence is the admission. So He heals the man and releases him, sending him out of the room before the argument starts, so that he does not have to stand there as an exhibit.

Then a guest begins telling everybody where to sit. Seating at a formal meal was a public ranking and every person there knew exactly what his place said about him. Read as etiquette the advice is shrewd and very nearly a quotation from Proverbs 25. But the text calls it a parable, which means the host in the story is not the Pharisee. There is another table and somebody else does the seating.

He then turns on the man who invited Him, in his own house, and goes after the guest list. Do not invite the people who can invite you back. That entire society ran on returned favours, and He is not adjusting the seating chart but unplugging the machine. Invite those who cannot repay, and be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous - which is to say, stop settling all the accounts here.

Somebody makes a pious noise about eating bread in the Kingdom, the sort of thing said when a conversation becomes uncomfortable, and is answered with a story in which every invited guest declines. Invitations worked in two stages: accepted in advance, then confirmed when the food was ready. These men had already said yes. And the excuses are respectable - a field, five yoke of oxen, a new wife - though nobody buys a field unseen or five pairs of oxen untested. They are not reasons but performances, and they echo Deuteronomy 20, where a new house, a new vineyard and a new wife excuse a man from the battle line. Torah exemptions from a war are being used to get out of a banquet.

The master's anger does not cancel the party; it enlarges it, first into the streets and lanes and then out beyond the walls. And the servant's report - there is still room - is the most hopeful line in the chapter. Then He turns to the growing crowd and begins subtracting. The word rendered hate is the Semitic comparative; Leah is the hated wife beside Rachel, and she was not hated but loved less, and Matthew renders the same saying as loves more than me. It is comparison, not cruelty - though His own life is on the list, and no idiom gets a reader out of that. Nobody in that crowd heard bear his own cross as a figure of speech; they had watched condemned men carry the beam up their own road. And the two little parables are not about caution. Both men are told to sit down and count, and the king with ten thousand against twenty thousand is never told how to win. He is told to send an envoy and ask for terms. Sometimes counting honestly ends in surrender to the stronger King, and that is not the failure but the point.

verses.1: When he went into the house of one of the rulers of the Pharisees on a Sabbath to eat bread, they were watching him.
verses.2: Behold, a certain man who had dropsy was in front of him.
verses.3: Jesus, answering, spoke to the lawyers and Pharisees, saying, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?”
verses.4: But they were silent. He took him, and healed him, and let him go.
verses.5: He answered them, “Which of you, if your son or an ox fell into a well, wouldn’t immediately pull him out on a Sabbath day?”
verses.6: They couldn’t answer him regarding these things.
verses.7: He spoke a parable to those who were invited, when he noticed how they chose the best seats, and said to them,
verses.8: “When you are invited by anyone to a marriage feast, don’t sit in the best seat, since perhaps someone more honorable than you might be invited by him,
verses.9: and he who invited both of you would come and tell you, ‘Make room for this person.’ Then you would begin, with shame, to take the lowest place.
verses.10: But when you are invited, go and sit in the lowest place, so that when he who invited you comes, he may tell you, ‘Friend, move up higher.’ Then you will be honored in the presence of all who sit at the table with you.
verses.11: For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.”
verses.12: He also said to the one who had invited him, “When you make a dinner or a supper, don’t call your friends, nor your brothers, nor your kinsmen, nor rich neighbors, or perhaps they might also return the favor, and pay you back.
verses.13: But when you make a feast, ask the poor, the maimed, the lame, or the blind;
verses.14: and you will be blessed, because they don’t have the resources to repay you. For you will be repaid in the resurrection of the righteous.”
verses.15: When one of those who sat at the table with him heard these things, he said to him, “Blessed is he who will feast in God’s Kingdom!”
verses.16: But he said to him, “A certain man made a great supper, and he invited many people.
verses.17: He sent out his servant at supper time to tell those who were invited, ‘Come, for everything is ready now.’
verses.18: They all as one began to make excuses. “The first said to him, ‘I have bought a field, and I must go and see it. Please have me excused.’
verses.19: “Another said, ‘I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I must go try them out. Please have me excused.’
verses.20: “Another said, ‘I have married a wife, and therefore I can’t come.’
verses.21: “That servant came, and told his lord these things. Then the master of the house, being angry, said to his servant, ‘Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in the poor, maimed, blind, and lame.’
verses.22: “The servant said, ‘Lord, it is done as you commanded, and there is still room.’
verses.23: “The lord said to the servant, ‘Go out into the highways and hedges, and compel them to come in, that my house may be filled.
verses.24: For I tell you that none of those men who were invited will taste of my supper.’”
verses.25: Now great multitudes were going with him. He turned and said to them,
verses.26: “If anyone comes to me, and doesn’t disregard his own father, mother, wife, children, brothers, and sisters, yes, and his own life also, he can’t be my disciple.
verses.27: Whoever doesn’t bear his own cross, and come after me, can’t be my disciple.
verses.28: For which of you, desiring to build a tower, doesn’t first sit down and count the cost, to see if he has enough to complete it?
verses.29: Or perhaps, when he has laid a foundation, and is not able to finish, everyone who sees begins to mock him,
verses.30: saying, ‘This man began to build, and wasn’t able to finish.’
verses.31: Or what king, as he goes to encounter another king in war, will not sit down first and consider whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand?
verses.32: Or else, while the other is yet a great way off, he sends an envoy, and asks for conditions of peace.
verses.33: So therefore whoever of you who doesn’t renounce all that he has, he can’t be my disciple.
verses.34: Salt is good, but if the salt becomes flat and tasteless, with what do you season it?
verses.35: It is fit neither for the soil nor for the manure pile. It is thrown out. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 15 - One Sheep, One Coin, and a Father Who Ran
chapters.title: One Sheep, One Coin, and a Father Who Ran
keyNotes: Verses 1 and 2 are the whole chapter. Three parables, one complaint: this man welcomes sinners and eats with them (Luke 15:1-3).
"Were coming close to him to hear him" is a continuing action - this was not a one-off scandal, it was the pattern of His ministry (Luke 15:1).
The offence is not that He talks to sinners. It is that He eats with them. At that table, sharing food was sharing standing (Luke 15:2).
"Which of you men, if you had one hundred sheep" - He starts by putting the Pharisees in the shepherd's place, and every one of them would say yes, of course I would go (Luke 15:4).
The ninety-nine are left "in the wilderness" - that is open pasture, not abandonment. Flocks were usually watched by more than one man (Luke 15:4).
"Until he found it." The search has no stated limit (Luke 15:4).
He carries it home on his shoulders, rejoicing. A grown sheep is a heavy load, and the sheep contributes nothing to the journey back (Luke 15:5).
Both of the first two parables end in a party, with neighbours called in. He is defending what He is doing at that very moment (Luke 15:6, 9).
"Ninety-nine righteous people who need no repentance" is said to men who believed that description fitted them. It is not a category He is endorsing; it is one He is quoting (Luke 15:7).
A drachma was about a day's wage. Ten of them may have been a woman's dowry set, sometimes worn as a headpiece - which would make the loss both financial and personal (Luke 15:8).
She lights a lamp and sweeps, because a first-century house had few windows and a floor of beaten earth and straw. The listening is for the sound of the coin moving (Luke 15:8).
The second parable puts a woman in the searching role, deliberately set beside the shepherd. God is imaged as both in one breath (Luke 15:8-10).
"Joy in the presence of the angels of God" is a careful phrase. The angels are the audience. The joy is God's own (Luke 15:10).
The third parable never says lost and found rejoicing about the older brother, and it never ends. That is the design (Luke 15:11, 32).
"Give me my share of your property" while the father lives is, at best, treating him as already dead. Ancient law made it possible; the culture made it unthinkable (Luke 15:12).
"He divided his livelihood between them" - the word is bios, his living, his life. And note both sons receive; the elder's share is already in his hands from this verse on (Luke 15:12).
The far country, the famine, and the pigs are a descending staircase. For a Jewish son, feeding pigs is the bottom step (Luke 15:13-15).
"No one gave him any" - the far country's hospitality summed up in five words (Luke 15:16).
"When he came to himself" is the language of return - the same idea the rabbis used for repentance, a man coming back to his right mind (Luke 15:17).

His prepared speech is half confession and half business plan. Make me one of your hired servants - a misthios is a paid day labourer, not a household slave. He is proposing to work the debt off (Luke 15:18-19).
"While he was still far off, his father saw him." You only see someone a long way off if you have been looking (Luke 15:20).
The father runs. A landowner of standing did not run - it meant gathering up his robe and showing his legs, which was a humiliation. He takes it in front of the whole village (Luke 15:20).
"Kissed him" is kataphileo - kissed him again and again. And it happens before a word of the speech is said (Luke 15:20).
The son gets out the confession but never gets to the proposal. The father cuts him off before "make me a hired servant." There is no arrangement where the boy earns his way back in (Luke 15:21-22).
Robe, ring, shoes: the best robe is the father's own, the ring carries authority, and shoes are what sons wear - the slaves in that house were barefoot. He is not reinstated as staff (Luke 15:22).
A fattened calf feeds far more than a family. The whole village is being invited to receive him back (Luke 15:23).
"Was dead, and is alive again; was lost, and is found" is said twice - once to the servants, once to the elder brother. The second time it is an argument (Luke 15:24, 32).
The elder son is in the field, which is exactly where a good son should be. Nothing in the story faults his work (Luke 15:25).
He will not go in, so the father comes out - and this is the second time in the parable the father leaves the house to go to a son (Luke 15:28).
"These many years I have served you" is douleuo - I have slaved for you. He has been living as a hired hand in a house where he was always a son (Luke 15:29).
"I never disobeyed a commandment of yours" is Torah language, spoken in a parable aimed at men who would have said the same (Luke 15:29).
"This your son" says the elder brother. "This your brother" answers the father. Neither of them uses the other's word (Luke 15:30, 32).
"Son, you are always with me" - the word is teknon, child. It is the tenderest address in the parable, and it is given to the angry one (Luke 15:31).
"All that is mine is yours" is literally true. The estate was divided in verse 12; the calf the elder is angry about was already his (Luke 15:31).
The story stops without telling us whether he goes in. The men who started the argument in verse 2 are handed the pen (Luke 15:32).

intro: Everything in this chapter hangs on two verses at the top. All the tax collectors and sinners were drawing near to hear Him, and the Pharisees and scribes grumbled that this man receives sinners and eats with them.

Eats with them is the charge. In that world a table was not merely food; whom a man ate with was whom he stood with. Preaching at sinners from a distance would have troubled nobody. Sitting down and eating with them says something about them, and about the man doing it.

So three parables, which are not three sermons but one answer told three times, each version longer and closer to the bone. The first puts the Pharisees in the shepherd's place and gets them agreeing before they know what they are agreeing to - of course a man goes after the one. And when he finds it he does not drive it home; he carries it on his shoulders, and a grown sheep is dead weight. That sheep contributes nothing to the journey back. Then a party.

The second sets a woman in the searching role deliberately beside the shepherd, so that no single picture of God can settle. One room, a beaten-earth floor, few windows; she is listening for the sound of the coin under the broom as much as looking. And when she finds it, the neighbours are called in. Another party - which is precisely what He is being accused of at that moment. He is not explaining Himself so much as telling them what the party is.

Then the third, and the gears change. Father, give me my share. There is no polite way to hear that; the son is asking his father to be dead. And the first shock, before any of the famous ones, is that the father does it - and divides his living between them both, which means everything remaining in that house already belongs to the elder brother from that verse onward. Then the descent: far country, wasted, famine, pigs, and the loneliest line in the chapter, that he longed to fill his stomach with what the pigs ate and no one gave him anything. That is the far country's hospitality; it took everything and would not feed him.

But when he came to himself. Not when he felt sorry - when he came back to his right mind, as though everything before it had been a kind of madness. His speech is half repentance and half business plan, because a hired man earns a wage and he is going home to work the debt off. And he never gets to that part. The father sees him a long way off, which means he had been watching; runs, which required an older man of standing to gather up his robe and make a fool of himself in front of the village; and interrupts the speech with a robe, a ring and shoes. The slaves in that house were barefoot. Every one of those things says the same thing: there is no arrangement here, and nothing is being worked off. Then the camera does not stop. The elder son is in the field, which is where a good son should be, and nothing in the story faults his work - but he has been living as an employee in a house where he was always a son, and nobody made him do it. He says this son of yours; the father says this brother of yours. And the word the father uses for him is the tenderest in the parable, and it is given to the angry one. The story stops without saying whether he went in, which is not a loose end but a question handed back to the men who started the argument in verse 2.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 16 - The Shrewd Manager, Two Masters, and a Beggar Whose Name He Knew
chapters.title: The Shrewd Manager, Two Masters, and a Beggar Whose Name He Knew
keyNotes: The parable is told to the disciples, but verse 14 tells us who else was listening. The whole chapter has two audiences (Luke 16:1, 14).
An oikonomos was not a servant with a broom. He was the estate manager - he signed contracts, held the accounts, and acted with his master's authority (Luke 16:1).
"Wasting his possessions" is diaskorpizo - the same verb Luke used one chapter earlier for the younger son squandering his inheritance. The two men are being set side by side (Luke 16:1, 15:13).
He is dismissed before he acts. "Give an accounting" means he still holds the books and the seal for a few more hours, and everything he does next happens inside that window (Luke 16:2).
"I don't have strength to dig. I am ashamed to beg" is an honest inventory. He knows exactly what he is and is not (Luke 16:3).
A hundred batos of oil is somewhere around eight hundred gallons; a hundred cors of wheat is the yield of a very large field. These are commercial accounts, not neighbours borrowing (Luke 16:6-7).
The two reductions look uneven - half the oil, a fifth of the wheat - but in money they come out close to the same. He is being precise, not generous (Luke 16:6-7).

Why the master commends him is the old question. The most common reading is that what he struck off was interest, or his own commission, so the master loses nothing and is publicly praised for generosity. The text does not say, and this book will not pretend it does (Luke 16:8).
Luke calls him the unrighteous manager in the same sentence in which the master praises him. The commendation is for shrewdness - phronimos - not for honesty (Luke 16:8).

"The children of this world are wiser in their own generation than the children of the light" is a comparison, and it is meant to sting. He is saying His own people are not thinking as hard about eternity as this man thought about next month (Luke 16:8).
"Make for yourselves friends by means of unrighteous mammon" - use what will not last to make relationships that will. The money is spent either way; the only question is on what (Luke 16:9).
Verses 10 to 12 are three tests: little and much, unrighteous mammon and true riches, another's and your own. Money is somebody else's property that passes through your hands (Luke 16:10-12).
Mammon is an Aramaic word for wealth, built on the root for trust - that in which you put confidence. In verse 13 it stops being a thing and becomes a rival master (Luke 16:9, 13).
"No servant can serve two masters." Roman law did allow joint ownership of a slave, so the problem is not the timetable. It is that both of these masters want everything (Luke 16:13).
The Pharisees "scoffed" - ekmukterizo, literally turned up the nose. Luke tells us plainly why: they were lovers of money (Luke 16:14).
"What is exalted among men is an abomination in the sight of God." Abomination is Torah's own word, and He aims it at respectability (Luke 16:15).
Verses 16 to 18 look like three unrelated sayings dropped in the middle. They are the hinge of the chapter: the law stands, the Kingdom is being announced, and here is a test case (Luke 16:16-18).

"Everyone is forcing his way into it" translates biazetai, a verb that can be read either as people pressing eagerly in or as the Kingdom being pressed violently. The WEB takes the first (Luke 16:16).

A keraia is the little hook that distinguishes one Hebrew letter from another. He says not one of them will fall in the same breath as He announces the Kingdom. Whatever is being superseded, the Torah is not being cancelled (Luke 16:17).
The divorce saying is placed here as evidence, not as a change of subject. Men who loved money also loved the loose reading of Deuteronomy 24, and He has just said the law does not bend (Luke 16:18).
In the last parable the beggar has a name and the rich man does not. That is unique in the parables, and it is a deliberate reversal of who gets remembered (Luke 16:19-20).
Lazarus is Eleazar - God has helped. The name is the sermon (Luke 16:20).
Purple dye and fine linen were imported luxuries, and "living in luxury every day" means he feasted daily at a level most people managed only at festivals (Luke 16:19).
"Was taken to his gate" - the man was carried there. Somebody put him where the rich man would walk past him every single day (Luke 16:20).
The dogs licking his sores are the only creatures in the story who come near him, and they are unclean animals (Luke 16:21).
"Abraham's bosom" is the place next to the host at a banquet - the seat of honour. The beggar who wanted crumbs is reclining at the table (Luke 16:22-23).
This is a parable about a state before the resurrection, not a survey of the final judgment. It is not built to answer every question we bring to it (Luke 16:23).
The rich man knows his name. He calls him Lazarus across the gulf, which means he knew it at the gate - and he still asks for him to be sent on an errand (Luke 16:24).
Abraham calls him "son" - teknon, child. His lineage is granted and it changes nothing (Luke 16:25).
"A great gulf fixed" is a perfect passive: it has been established and it stands (Luke 16:26).
His last request is the first unselfish thing he says - and it is still an instruction about what Lazarus should do (Luke 16:27-28).
"They have Moses and the prophets. Let them listen to them." The Scriptures they already hold are treated as sufficient warning (Luke 16:29).
The final line is spoken by a man who will rise from the dead, about people who will not be persuaded by it. Luke's readers know how that turned out (Luke 16:31).

intro: This is the parable readers skip. A rich man has an estate manager - not a servant with a broom but a man who signs contracts in his master's name and keeps the books - and word gets back that he is wasting the property. The verb is the one used a chapter earlier for the prodigal squandering his inheritance, which is not an accident. One man has just wasted what was given him; here is another.

He is dismissed before he acts, and that is the hinge. Give an account of your management means he still holds the books and the seal for a few more hours, and everyone who owes the estate still believes he speaks for the master. So he does the arithmetic on his own life, and produces one of the most honest sentences in the Gospels: I cannot dig, and I am ashamed to beg. He knows exactly what he is.

Then the debtors, and the numbers are commercial rather than neighbourly - eight hundred gallons of oil, the yield of a very large wheat field - and the two discounts, uneven on paper, come out close to the same in money. He is not being generous; he is being exact. And the master commends him. Not for honesty; the text calls him unrighteous in the same sentence. For being awake. He saw a crisis coming, knew he could not stop it, and used the only window he had to prepare for the day after. The children of this age are shrewder in dealing with their own generation than the children of light, which is a comparison meant to sting.

The tests that follow turn on faithfulness: little and much, unrighteous mammon and true riches, another's and your own. That last one says plainly what He thinks money is - it belongs to somebody else and is passing through the hands that hold it. And in verse 13 mammon stops being a thing and becomes a rival with a claim.

Three sentences then look like a change of subject and are not. The law and the prophets were until John, and the Kingdom is now announced - and in the very next breath, it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one tiny hook of a letter to fall from the law. Whatever the first sentence means, it does not mean the Torah is finished, and the divorce saying is the exhibit rather than a new topic. Men who were loose with money were also loose with Deuteronomy 24, and He has just said the law does not bend.

In the last parable the beggar has a name and the rich man does not, which happens nowhere else in the parables and reverses the way that street worked. Lazarus is Eleazar - God has helped. Purple and fine linen were imported luxuries and he feasted daily at a level most people managed only at festivals, while a man was carried to his gate and laid where he would walk past him, with unclean animals supplying the only care he received. And the conversation across the gulf convicts, because the rich man knows his name. He calls him Lazarus, which means he knew it at the gate, every day - and he is still trying to send him on errands. Abraham grants the lineage and denies the request. The last exchange is the point: they have Moses and the prophets, and if they will not hear them, neither will they be persuaded though one rise from the dead - a sentence whose speaker did rise, about people who were not persuaded.
