chapters.heading: CHAPTER 17 - Unworthy Servants, One Who Came Back, and a Day That Looks Like an Ordinary Tuesday
chapters.title: Unworthy Servants, One Who Came Back, and a Day That Looks Like an Ordinary Tuesday
keyNotes: A skandalon was the baited stick that springs a trap. He says the traps are certain to come; the woe belongs to whoever sets them (Luke 17:1).
The millstone is the mulikos - the big one turned by a donkey, not the hand mill. Drowning weighted with a stone was a real Roman execution, so nobody heard this as a figure of speech (Luke 17:2).
"These little ones" in context is not only children. It is anyone whose footing is not yet sure (Luke 17:2).
"If your brother sins against you, rebuke him." The rebuke is commanded, not optional. Saying nothing is not the same as forgiving (Luke 17:3).
"If he repents, forgive him" - and then seven times in one day, with a claim of repentance each time. He gives no instruction for testing whether the seventh one is sincere (Luke 17:4).
The apostles hear all that and say increase our faith. It is the response of men who have just been handed something they know they cannot do (Luke 17:5).
He refuses the request as they framed it. Not more faith - faith the size of the smallest seed they know. The problem was never the quantity (Luke 17:6).
The sycamine is a mulberry, proverbial for deep roots, and He tells it to plant itself in the sea, where no tree grows. The picture is doubly impossible on purpose (Luke 17:6).
The servant parable follows immediately, and that placement is the point: the moment faith starts working, the temptation is to send God an invoice (Luke 17:7-10).
"Unworthy servants" is achreios - without claim, unprofitable. It is not self-loathing; it is an accurate statement about who owes whom (Luke 17:10).
"We have done our duty" is opheilomen - we have done what we owed. Obedience does not put God in our debt (Luke 17:10).
"Along the borders of Samaria and Galilee" is a border zone, which is exactly where a mixed colony of Jewish and Samaritan lepers would be possible (Luke 17:11-12).
"Stood at a distance" is Torah being kept. Leviticus requires it. These ten men are obeying the law that excludes them (Luke 17:12).
"Master" here is epistata, Luke's own word, used elsewhere in this Gospel only by disciples (Luke 17:13).
He gives them the Leviticus 14 procedure - go show yourselves to the priests - before anything has changed. They are healed while walking to a priest with nothing to show him (Luke 17:14).
One comes back, and Luke holds the detail to the very end of the sentence: and he was a Samaritan (Luke 17:16).
The nine were not disobedient - they were doing what He said. The Samaritan is the one who could not have completed that errand in Jerusalem anyway (Luke 17:14, 16).
"Your faith has healed you" is sozo - saved, made whole. Ten were cleansed; one is told something more (Luke 17:19).
"Doesn't come with observation" is parateresis - watching for signs, the same root as the Pharisees watching Him at dinner. The people asking are the ones described by the word (Luke 17:20, 14:1).
"Within you" translates entos hymon. Spoken to Pharisees, "among you" or "in your midst" is at least as likely as "inside you," and the difference matters. The WEB prints within (Luke 17:21).
"You will desire to see one of the days of the Son of Man, and you will not see it" - a warning that the waiting itself will get hard (Luke 17:22).
Lightning needs no guide. If somebody has to point it out to you and tell you where to look, that is the tell (Luke 17:23-24).
"But first he must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation." The cross is set down in the middle of the end-times teaching, not beside it (Luke 17:25).

Read the list of what Noah's and Lot's neighbours were doing: eating, drinking, marrying, buying, selling, planting, building. Not one scandal among them. The danger is normality that has stopped listening (Luke 17:27-28).
"Remember Lot's wife" is three words, and the shortest sentence in Luke. She did not go back. She only looked back (Luke 17:32).
"Let him not go down to take his goods" - the housetop was flat, with an outside stair. The instruction is to leave by the roof and not step back inside for anything (Luke 17:31).
Two in a bed, two grinding together - pairs doing identical things, and the separation runs between them. Nothing external distinguishes the two (Luke 17:34-35).

Verse 36 is absent from the WEB. The footnote records that some Greek manuscripts add "two will be in the field: the one taken, and the other left," carried over from Matthew. The chapter runs 1 to 37 with 36 unprinted (Luke 17:36).
"Where, Lord?" gets an answer about vultures gathering over a body. The Greek word can mean eagle or vulture. Either way the answer is: you will not need directions (Luke 17:37).

intro: The chapter opens with a warning that is not taken seriously often enough. Occasions of stumbling are certain to come, but woe to the one through whom they come. The word is skandalon, and it is not a stone tripped over by accident; it is the baited stick that springs a trap. And the sentence attached to it is a millstone - the large one, turned by a donkey, not the hand mill.

Then the rebuke is commanded rather than permitted. Christians have a habit of calling silence forgiveness when it is really avoidance; the instruction is to say something. And if he repents, forgive - seven times in one day, with a claim of repentance each time, and no test of sincerity offered anywhere.

The apostles' response to that is the most human line in the chapter: increase our faith. They have just been handed something they know they cannot do, and they ask for more of whatever it takes. He refuses the request as framed. Faith the size of the smallest seed they know could uproot a mulberry - a tree proverbial for its roots - and plant it in salt water. The picture is doubly impossible on purpose. The question was never how much.

The servant parable follows immediately, and the placement is the argument: the moment faith begins to work, the temptation is to send God an invoice. Unworthy servants does not mean self- hatred. It means without a claim. We have done what we owed.

Then the border country between Samaria and Galilee, which is exactly where a mixed colony of lepers becomes possible, because the disease did not respect the boundary. Ten men stand at the distance Leviticus requires - keeping the law that excludes them - and are sent to the priests before anything has changed, which means ten sick men walking toward a certification for a healing that has not happened. They are cleansed on the road, in the obedience, and not before it. One turns back, and Luke holds the detail to the last four words of the sentence: and he was a Samaritan. The nine were not disobedient; they were doing what He said. But to them nothing further was spoken, and to this one: your faith has made you whole. Ten were cleansed. One was saved.

The Pharisees ask when the Kingdom will come, and the word behind His answer, observation, shares a root with the watching they did at that Sabbath dinner. The Kingdom does not come by the kind of looking they are doing. And within you may equally be rendered among you or in your midst; spoken to that particular audience, with Him standing there, the second is hard to argue with. Then the days of the Son of Man, which will be missed by the people waiting for them, and a warning against anyone who has to point and say look here - because nobody needs a guide to see lightning. And in the middle of the end of the world He sets the cross: but first He must suffer many things. Then Noah's neighbours and Lot's, and what they were doing when it fell - eating, drinking, marrying, buying, selling, planting, building. There is not a scandal on the list. That is the warning. It was not that they were monstrous but that everything was entirely normal, right up until it was not.

verses.4: If he sins against you seven times in the day, and seven times returns, saying, ‘I repent,’ you shall forgive him.”

verses.9: Does he thank that servant because he did the things that were commanded? I think not.
verses.10: Even so you also, when you have done all the things that are commanded you, say, ‘We are unworthy servants. We have done our duty.’”

verses.26: As it was in the days of Noah, even so will it be also in the days of the Son of Man.

verses.32: Remember Lot’s wife!
verses.33: Whoever seeks to save his life loses it, but whoever loses his life preserves it.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 18 - The Widow Who Wore Him Down, the Man Who Would Not Look Up, and the Beggar Who Got Louder
chapters.title: The Widow Who Wore Him Down, the Man Who Would Not Look Up, and the Beggar Who Got Louder
keyNotes: Luke tells us the point before the parable starts - that they ought always to pray and not give up. He rarely does that, so when he does, take the hint (Luke 18:1).
"Didn't fear God, and didn't respect man" was a stock description of a shameless official. In a Jewish town, a judge who fits it is probably not a Torah judge at all (Luke 18:2).
A widow is the textbook defenceless litigant - no husband to speak for her, no leverage, and no money for the bribe the situation clearly wanted (Luke 18:3).
"Defend me" is ekdikeo - give me justice, vindicate me. She is not asking him to punish her adversary. She is asking for a ruling (Luke 18:3).
"She will wear me out" is hupopiazo - a boxing word, to give someone a black eye. Whether he fears an actual scene or the damage to his face in public, he gives in to protect himself (Luke 18:5).
The argument runs from lesser to greater: if a judge like that eventually rules, how much more the Father. The parable works by contrast, not by comparison (Luke 18:6-7).
"Yet he exercises patience with them" is the hard clause. The delay is not indifference and it is not weakness - it is long-suffering, and it is aimed somewhere (Luke 18:7).
"He will avenge them quickly" sits in the same breath as "crying out day and night." Both are true, and they are measuring time differently (Luke 18:7-8).
The last line turns the whole parable around: when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on the earth? The question was never whether God would answer (Luke 18:8).
Luke again names the audience before the parable: those convinced of their own righteousness, who despised all others. Both halves of that matter (Luke 18:9).
"Two men went up into the temple to pray" - most likely one of the set hours of prayer, when the atonement sacrifice was offered (Luke 18:10).
"Prayed to himself" can be read as stood by himself and prayed, or prayed to himself. Both readings describe what actually happened (Luke 18:11).
The Pharisee's prayer contains no request. It is a report, and it is accurate - fasting twice a week and tithing everything both go beyond what Torah requires (Luke 18:11-12).
The tax collector stands far off, like a leper. He beats his breast, a gesture of grief rare enough in men to be worth Luke recording (Luke 18:13).
"Be merciful to me" is hilaskomai - be propitiated, let atonement be made. He is standing in the one place on earth where that word had a smoking altar behind it (Luke 18:13).
He says "the sinner," with the definite article - not one among many. In his own accounting he is the case (Luke 18:13).
"Went down to his house justified" is dikaioo, a courtroom verdict. Paul builds a whole vocabulary on this word, and here it is in a parable (Luke 18:14).
The babies are brephos - infants. Bringing children to an elder for a blessing was ordinary Jewish practice; the disciples are the ones being strange (Luke 18:15).
"Receive the Kingdom like a little child" - a child in that world had no standing, no leverage, and nothing to trade. Receiving is the only thing available to them (Luke 18:17).
"Good Teacher" was flattery, not a creed. His reply is not a denial of His goodness; it is a question about whether the ruler meant what he just said (Luke 18:18-19).
He lists the second table of the commandments - the ones about your neighbour - and leaves out the one about coveting. That is the one about to be tested (Luke 18:20).
"I have observed all these things from my youth up." Nothing in the text says he is lying (Luke 18:21).
The instruction has four parts and the first three serve the fourth: sell, distribute, then come, follow me. The money is the obstacle, not the object (Luke 18:22).
"He became very sad, for he was very rich." Luke never says he refused - only that he grieved. The story is left open the way the elder brother's was (Luke 18:23).
The camel and the needle's eye. There is a popular tale about a small gate in Jerusalem called the Needle's Eye; there is no evidence such a gate existed. He meant it to be impossible (Luke 18:25).
"Then who can be saved?" only makes sense if you assume wealth is a mark of God's favour - which is exactly what they assumed (Luke 18:26).
"What is impossible with men is possible with God" is the only answer given, and it is the answer to the rich man's problem and to ours (Luke 18:27).
Peter's inventory - we have left our own - gets a promise that includes this present time as well as the age to come. Luke alone lists a wife among what is left (Luke 18:28-30).
The third and fullest passion prediction, and the only one that grounds it in the prophets: everything written through them concerning the Son of Man will be completed (Luke 18:31).
"Delivered up to the Gentiles" is new information in Luke's account, and it is the detail that makes a Roman cross rather than a stoning (Luke 18:32).

Luke says the same thing three ways in one verse - they understood none of it, it was hidden from them, they did not grasp what was said. He is protecting the disciples from a charge of stupidity: it was hidden (Luke 18:34).

Mark names this beggar Bartimaeus and puts the healing as they leave Jericho; Matthew has two men. Luke has it as He approaches. There was an old Jericho and a new one and the road ran between them, which may account for it - this book flags the difference rather than smoothing it (Luke 18:35).
"Son of David" is the first time in Luke that anybody shouts a messianic title at Him in public - and it is a blind beggar, on the road up to Jerusalem (Luke 18:38).
They rebuke him to be quiet, exactly as they rebuked the people bringing babies. He gets louder (Luke 18:39, 15).
"What do you want me to do?" - asked of a man whose need is the most obvious thing about him. He makes him say it (Luke 18:41).
"Your faith has healed you" is the same word spoken to the Samaritan leper one chapter earlier. And the man does not go home; he follows Him up the road (Luke 18:42-43).

intro: Luke does something here he almost never does: he states the point before he tells the parable. They ought always to pray and not lose heart.

The judge neither feared God nor respected people, which was a set phrase for a certain kind of official - immune to heaven and to public opinion alike. And a widow means no husband to speak for her in court, no standing, and no money for the bribe the situation was plainly asking for. She keeps coming, and what she asks for is a ruling rather than revenge. What finally moves him is described with a boxing term: she will give him a black eye. He is afraid of her.

The parable works by contrast rather than comparison. He is not saying God resembles that judge; He is saying that if even that man eventually rules, how much more the Father. The widow's only weapon was that she would not go away. And yet the two halves of the answer sit strangely together - He is patient with them, and He will vindicate them speedily, said of people crying out day and night. Both are true, and time is being measured differently, which is exactly what makes the waiting hard. Then the sentence that turns the parable inside out: when the Son of Man comes, will He find faith on the earth? The question was never whether He would answer.

Two men go up to the temple, and again the audience is named first: those who trusted in themselves that they were righteous and treated others with contempt. Both halves matter. It is not only the confidence; it is what the confidence does to the way a person looks at whoever is standing next to him.

The Pharisee's prayer contains no request anywhere in it. It is a report - and everything in it is true. Fasting twice a week exceeds what the law asks; tithing everything he receives exceeds it too. He is not a fraud, and that is what makes the passage uncomfortable. The tax collector stands at the distance the lepers kept, will not lift his eyes, and beats his breast, and the word he uses is not the ordinary one for mercy but the word for atonement - let the blood count for me. He is standing in the one place on earth where an altar was smoking for exactly that. And he says the sinner, with the article, as though he were the only one in the building.

Children are brought to be blessed, which was a perfectly ordinary thing to do with a rabbi, and the disciples try to stop it. A child in that world had no rights, no leverage and nothing to trade; receiving is the only thing available. And Luke sets the rich ruler immediately beside that, because the baby can only receive and the ruler wants to know the price. The commandments listed are the ones about neighbours, and the one left off the list is the one about coveting. He is not told to give it away and go, but to sell, distribute, and then come and follow - three instructions serving a fourth. And Luke never says he refused. He says he became sad, and leaves the door open the way he left the elder brother's open. The camel and the needle is meant to be impossible, whatever is said about gates in Jerusalem, for which there is no evidence. Who then can be saved is a sensible question if wealth is a sign of blessing, and the only answer given is the one that covers everybody: what is impossible with men is possible with God.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 19 - A Rich Man Up a Tree, a Mina in a Handkerchief, and a King Who Wept
chapters.title: A Rich Man Up a Tree, a Mina in a Handkerchief, and a King Who Wept
keyNotes: Zacchaeus is Zakkai - pure, righteous, innocent. Whatever his parents hoped for, the town had long since stopped using the name that way (Luke 19:2).

"Chief tax collector" - architelones - appears nowhere else in surviving Greek. He was a contractor with collectors working under him, and Jericho, on the balsam trade and the crossing into Perea, was a rich posting (Luke 19:2).
Luke says plainly that he was rich, one chapter after the rich ruler walked away sad. The two stories are meant to be read against each other (Luke 19:2, 18:23).
"He was short" - the Greek says small in stature and is grammatically ambiguous about which man is meant. The natural reading is Zacchaeus, and that is how the WEB takes it (Luke 19:3).
A sycamore here is the fig-mulberry, a broad tree with low branches. Easy to climb - and a wealthy man in a tree is undignified in any century (Luke 19:4).
"Today I must stay at your house." The must is dei, the word Luke uses for divine necessity, the same word used of the cross (Luke 19:5).
"They all murmured" is diagogguzo, the Greek Old Testament's word for Israel grumbling in the wilderness. Luke is putting the crowd in a role they would not have chosen (Luke 19:7).
Zacchaeus "stood" to speak. That is the posture of a formal declaration, not a private apology. This is a vow made in front of witnesses (Luke 19:8).

Half to the poor is beyond any requirement. And fourfold restitution is the penalty for stolen livestock - the harshest bracket in the law. For fraud, Torah asks the principal plus a fifth. He sentences himself under the strictest category available (Luke 19:8).

The verbs are present tense - I give, I restore - which can be read as a new decision made on the spot or as a defence of what he already does. The first is the natural sense here, and it is how the WEB reads it (Luke 19:8).
"He also is a son of Abraham" answers the crowd on their own ground, and echoes the daughter of Abraham bent double in the synagogue (Luke 19:9, 13:16).
Verse 10 is the thesis of the whole Gospel, and Luke lets it land on a rich man - the outcome the ruler in the last chapter did not reach (Luke 19:10).
Luke tells us why the next parable is told: they were near Jerusalem and supposed the Kingdom was about to appear. It is a brake, not a timetable (Luke 19:11).

The nobleman going abroad to be given a kingdom is not invented. Archelaus sailed to Rome to be confirmed as king, and a Jewish delegation followed to argue against him. His palace was in Jericho - they were standing in his town (Luke 19:12, 14).
A mina is a hundred denarii, roughly three months' wages. Ten servants get one each - the same amount to everyone, unlike the differing talents in Matthew (Luke 19:13).
Only three of the ten report. The parable is not interested in the other seven, and it is least interested in the two who succeeded (Luke 19:16-20).
The third servant did not lose the money or spend it. He preserved it perfectly, wrapped in a cloth. Preservation is the failure (Luke 19:20).
"You are an exacting man" - austeros, severe. That picture of the master is what paralysed him, and it is the real subject of the parable (Luke 19:21).
"Out of your own mouth will I judge you." The master never agrees with the description; he argues from inside it. If you really believed that, you would at least have used a bank (Luke 19:22-23).

The banking detail is a reminder that a parable is not an allegory in every particular. Torah forbids charging a brother interest, and the master in the story is a Gentile-style ruler on his way back from Rome (Luke 19:23).

Verse 27 is brutal, and it is Archelaus to the letter - he came home and killed the men who petitioned against him. Whatever else it is, it is the historical picture the parable has been using throughout (Luke 19:27).

Bethphage, Bethany and the Mount of Olives are named together deliberately. That mountain is where Zechariah says Yahweh's feet will stand, and it is where David went up weeping when his own kingdom was taken from him (Luke 19:29).
A colt that no one has ever ridden is the requirement for an animal put to sacred use - the red heifer, the cart for the ark (Luke 19:30).
"The Lord needs it" is the whole explanation given, and it works. Whether that was arranged beforehand, Luke does not say (Luke 19:31, 34).
Luke has no palm branches and no Hosanna. Only cloaks in the road - which is what Israel did when Jehu was proclaimed king (Luke 19:36).
It is "the whole multitude of the disciples" who shout, not the city. Luke is careful about that, and it changes how you read the crowd later in the week (Luke 19:37).
They quote Psalm 118 and add one word: blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord. The word they add is the one He will be crucified for (Luke 19:38).
"Peace in heaven and glory in the highest" answers the angels at His birth, who said peace on earth. Between the two, something has moved (Luke 19:38, 2:14).
"The stones would cry out" is Habakkuk, where the stone cries out of the wall against a city built on blood. It is not a charming image; it is an indictment (Luke 19:40).
"He wept" is klaio - to wail out loud. It is the word for public mourning, not for quiet tears (Luke 19:41).
"The things which belong to your peace" is a play on the city's own name. Jerusalem did not know the peace it was named for (Luke 19:42).
Verses 43 and 44 describe siege works - a palisade, an encirclement, children dashed to the ground. Titus built exactly that in the spring of AD 70 (Luke 19:43-44).
"You didn't know the time of your visitation" - episkope, the word for an inspection or an overseer's visit. The tragedy is not that God stayed away (Luke 19:44).
Luke gives the temple cleansing two verses. No whip, no overturned tables described - just the quotation and then daily teaching (Luke 19:45-47).
The sentence is stitched from Isaiah and Jeremiah, and Isaiah's line continues "for all peoples" - which is the exact court the market was standing in (Luke 19:46).
A den is not where robbers rob. It is where they go afterwards to feel safe (Luke 19:46).

intro: Nineteen chapters of walking end in this one, but not before Jericho and a man named Zacchaeus. The name means pure, righteous, innocent. Somebody named that child in hope, and by the time the Gospel reaches him the town would have said it with a curl of the lip.

He is a chief tax collector, which is not a booth on a road but a contractor who has bought the franchise and has other collectors working under him, in one of the wealthiest posts in the country. Rich, hated and successful. And Luke has just shown a rich ruler walk away sad, so the two men are meant to be held side by side. Wanting to see and unable to because of the crowd, a wealthy grown man in a good robe runs ahead and climbs a tree, which men of his standing did not do.

He is called by name and told that today, of necessity, this house is where He will stay - and the word for necessity is the one Luke uses of the cross. The grumbling that follows is described with the verb the Greek Old Testament uses for Israel murmuring in the wilderness. Then Zacchaeus stands, which is the posture of a formal declaration rather than a private apology, and makes a vow in front of the house: half of his goods to the poor, and fourfold restitution for anything defrauded. Fourfold is the penalty in Exodus for a stolen sheep; for fraud the law asks the principal plus a fifth. He reaches past the bracket he qualifies for and sentences himself under the harshest one available, unasked. And the answer names him a son of Abraham in front of a crowd that had written him out of the family, before the sentence the whole Gospel has been building toward: the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost - said over a rich man.

The parable that follows has its reason stated: they were near Jerusalem and supposed the Kingdom was about to appear. It is a story about the wait, and its setting was not invented. A nobleman who goes abroad to receive a kingdom while his own citizens send a delegation against him is Archelaus, within living memory, and his palace was in Jericho. Ten servants receive the same amount each. Three report. The third has not lost the money or spent it - he preserved it perfectly, wrapped in a cloth, and preservation is the failure. His reason is that he was afraid, because the master is a severe man, and that is what the parable is actually about: what he believed about his master is what froze his hands. The master never concedes the description. He argues from inside it - if that is really what you thought, why not at least a bank.

Then the road up, past Bethphage and Bethany and the Mount of Olives, the hill where Zechariah says His feet will stand and the hill David climbed weeping when his throne was taken. A colt no one has ridden is not a detail about transport but the specification for an animal set apart for sacred use. Cloaks go on the animal and then on the road, as Israel did when Jehu was made king.

Luke has no palm branches and no Hosanna, and it is the whole multitude of the disciples who shout rather than the city - which changes how the crowd later in the week should be read. What they shout is Psalm 118 with one word added: blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord. That word is the charge that will hang above His head. And where the angels said peace on earth at His birth, the disciples say peace in heaven on the donkey; something has moved between the two. Told to silence them, He answers with Habakkuk, where the stone cries out of the wall against a city built on blood - not a charming image but an indictment. Then the turn in the road where the whole city comes into view, and He wails aloud, the way people mourn at a graveside, over a city named for the peace it did not recognise, and describes a palisade and an encirclement forty years before Titus built one.

verses.1: He entered and was passing through Jericho.
verses.2: There was a man named Zacchaeus. He was a chief tax collector, and he was rich.
verses.3: He was trying to see who Jesus was, and couldn’t because of the crowd, because he was short.
verses.4: He ran on ahead, and climbed up into a sycamore tree to see him, for he was going to pass that way.
verses.5: When Jesus came to the place, he looked up and saw him, and said to him, “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must stay at your house.”
verses.6: He hurried, came down, and received him joyfully.
verses.7: When they saw it, they all murmured, saying, “He has gone in to lodge with a man who is a sinner.”
verses.8: Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, “Behold, Lord, half of my goods I give to the poor. If I have wrongfully exacted anything of anyone, I restore four times as much.”
verses.9: Jesus said to him, “Today, salvation has come to this house, because he also is a son of Abraham.
verses.10: For the Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost.”
verses.11: As they heard these things, he went on and told a parable, because he was near Jerusalem, and they supposed that God’s Kingdom would be revealed immediately.
verses.12: He said therefore, “A certain nobleman went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom, and to return.
verses.13: He called ten servants of his, and gave them ten mina coins, and told them, ‘Conduct business until I come.’
verses.14: But his citizens hated him, and sent an envoy after him, saying, ‘We don’t want this man to reign over us.’
verses.15: “When he had come back again, having received the kingdom, he commanded these servants, to whom he had given the money, to be called to him, that he might know what they had gained by conducting business.
verses.16: The first came before him, saying, ‘Lord, your mina has made ten more minas.’
verses.17: “He said to him, ‘Well done, you good servant! Because you were found faithful with very little, you shall have authority over ten cities.’
verses.18: “The second came, saying, ‘Your mina, Lord, has made five minas.’
verses.19: “So he said to him, ‘And you are to be over five cities.’
verses.20: Another came, saying, ‘Lord, behold, your mina, which I kept laid away in a handkerchief,
verses.21: for I feared you, because you are an exacting man. You take up that which you didn’t lay down, and reap that which you didn’t sow.’
verses.22: “He said to him, ‘Out of your own mouth will I judge you, you wicked servant! You knew that I am an exacting man, taking up that which I didn’t lay down, and reaping that which I didn’t sow.
verses.23: Then why didn’t you deposit my money in the bank, and at my coming, I might have earned interest on it?’
verses.24: He said to those who stood by, ‘Take the mina away from him, and give it to him who has the ten minas.’
verses.25: “They said to him, ‘Lord, he has ten minas!’
verses.26: ‘For I tell you that to everyone who has, will more be given; but from him who doesn’t have, even that which he has will be taken away from him.
verses.27: But bring those enemies of mine who didn’t want me to reign over them here, and kill them before me.’”
verses.28: Having said these things, he went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem.
verses.29: When he came near to Bethsphage and Bethany, at the mountain that is called Olivet, he sent two of his disciples,
verses.30: saying, “Go your way into the village on the other side, in which, as you enter, you will find a colt tied, which no man had ever sat upon. Untie it, and bring it.
verses.31: If anyone asks you, ‘Why are you untying it?’ say to him: ‘The Lord needs it.’”
verses.32: Those who were sent went away, and found things just as he had told them.
verses.33: As they were untying the colt, its owners said to them, “Why are you untying the colt?”
verses.34: They said, “The Lord needs it.”
verses.35: They brought it to Jesus. They threw their cloaks on the colt, and set Jesus on them.
verses.36: As he went, they spread their cloaks on the road.
verses.37: As he was now getting near, at the descent of the Mount of Olives, the whole multitude of the disciples began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works which they had seen,
verses.38: saying, “Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven, and glory in the highest!”
verses.39: Some of the Pharisees from the multitude said to him, “Teacher, rebuke your disciples!”
verses.40: He answered them, “I tell you that if these were silent, the stones would cry out.”
verses.41: When he came near, he saw the city and wept over it,
verses.42: saying, “If you, even you, had known today the things which belong to your peace! But now, they are hidden from your eyes.
verses.43: For the days will come on you, when your enemies will throw up a barricade against you, surround you, hem you in on every side,
verses.44: and will dash you and your children within you to the ground. They will not leave in you one stone on another, because you didn’t know the time of your visitation.”
verses.45: He entered into the temple, and began to drive out those who bought and sold in it,
verses.46: saying to them, “It is written, ‘My house is a house of prayer,’ but you have made it a ‘den of robbers’!”
verses.47: He was teaching daily in the temple, but the chief priests and the scribes and the leading men among the people sought to destroy him.
verses.48: They couldn’t find what they might do, for all the people hung on to every word that he said.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 20 - By What Authority, the Stone the Builders Threw Away, and Whose Face Is on the Coin
chapters.title: By What Authority, the Stone the Builders Threw Away, and Whose Face Is on the Coin
keyNotes: The delegation is the full council - chief priests, scribes and elders. This is not a debating party; it is an official inquiry (Luke 20:1).
"By what authority do you do these things?" has the temple action in view. They are asking for His credentials, and the honest answer would have ended the conversation (Luke 20:2).
The counter-question about John is not a dodge. John's authority and His come from the same place, so answering one answers the other (Luke 20:3-4).
Read their huddle again: both branches are political. Neither one asks whether John was actually sent by God (Luke 20:5-6).
"All the people will stone us" is fear talking, and it tells you who really held the ground that week (Luke 20:6).
"We don't know" is a lie, and He answers a lie with a refusal rather than an argument (Luke 20:7-8).
The vineyard parable is Isaiah 5 with a new ending. His hearers knew that song, so they knew who the vineyard was before He reached the tenants (Luke 20:9).
Luke sends the servants one at a time, with the violence escalating - beaten, beaten and shamed, wounded and thrown out. The owner's patience is the strange thing in the story (Luke 20:10-12).
"My beloved son" is the voice from the baptism and from the mountain. Luke's readers have heard those words twice already (Luke 20:13, 3:22, 9:35).
"They threw him out of the vineyard, and killed him." Luke puts the throwing out first. He was crucified outside the city wall (Luke 20:15).
"May it never be!" is the strongest negative in Greek. They understood the parable perfectly - verse 19 says so (Luke 20:16, 19).
Psalm 118 again, seven verses after the disciples sang it on the road. The crowd quoted the blessing; He quotes the rejected stone from the same psalm (Luke 20:17, 19:38).
The stone that breaks and the stone that crushes fuses Isaiah's stone of stumbling with Daniel's stone cut without hands. Both endings are in view (Luke 20:18).
The spies "pretended to be righteous." Luke tells us the disguise before he tells us the question (Luke 20:20).
Everything the spies say in verse 21 is true. Flattery does not have to be false to be a weapon (Luke 20:21).
The tax is the poll tax, payable only in Roman coin, and it had been the trigger for open revolt within living memory. There was no safe answer (Luke 20:22).
"Show me a denarius." He does not have one. The coin has to be produced by His questioners, in the temple courts (Luke 20:24).
The denarius carried Tiberius's head and an inscription naming him son of the divine Augustus and high priest. They are carrying that in the temple and asking Him about lawfulness (Luke 20:24).
"Give back" is apodidomi - return what is already his. The coin carries Caesar's image; the second half of the sentence assumes you know what carries God's (Luke 20:25, Genesis 1:27).
The Sadducees held only the five books of Moses as decisive and denied the resurrection - which is why His answer will come from Exodus and not from Daniel (Luke 20:27).
The levirate law is Deuteronomy 25. The seven-brother scenario is a debating-school case, not a real family (Luke 20:28-33).
His answer refuses the premise. The question assumes the age to come is a continuation of this one, with the same arrangements (Luke 20:34-35).
"They are like the angels" is explained in the same breath: they cannot die any more. Deathlessness is the point of comparison (Luke 20:36).
"Children of the resurrection" is a Semitic way of saying they belong to it - the same construction as sons of light (Luke 20:36).
Then He proves the resurrection from the burning bush - inside the Torah, on Sadducee ground. The argument rides on a tense: I am the God of Abraham (Luke 20:37).
"All are alive to him" is Luke's line and nobody else's (Luke 20:38).
"Teacher, you speak well" comes from scribes watching Sadducees lose an argument. He has won it with a text they accept (Luke 20:39-40).
Then He asks His own question and never answers it. Psalm 110: David calls him Lord - so how is he his son? It is left standing in the room (Luke 20:41-44).
Psalm 110 is the passage the New Testament quotes more than any other. It starts here, with a question nobody would answer (Luke 20:42-43).
The warning about the scribes is about costume and seating - long robes, greetings, best seats, best places. Everything on the list is about being seen (Luke 20:46).
"Devour widows' houses" most likely points at the abuse of estates entrusted to them. Torah puts widows under God's own protection, which makes it the worst possible target (Luke 20:47).
"Greater condemnation" is the last phrase before Luke shows us a widow putting in everything she has. He did not put a chapter break there; our Bibles did (Luke 20:47, 21:2).

intro: He is teaching in the temple daily now and the leadership has run out of patience, so they come as a delegation - chief priests, scribes and elders, which is the council. By what authority do you do these things is a fair question if it is asked honestly. He came into their courts and shut down the trading; somebody was going to ask.

He does not answer it, and the counter-question is not a dodge. Was the baptism of John from heaven or from men is the same question, because if John was sent by God then John's testimony settles the matter. And their huddle is one of the most damning conversations in the Gospel: if we say from heaven he will ask why we did not believe him, and if we say from men the people will stone us. Not one word about whether it was true. Both options are calculations about consequences. So they say they do not know, which is a lie, and a lie is answered with a refusal rather than an argument.

The vineyard parable opens with a quotation. A man planted a vineyard is Isaiah 5, the song of the vineyard, and every person present could have finished it, so they know who the vineyard is before He reaches the tenants. The servants come one at a time and the violence escalates, and the strange thing in the story is not the tenants but the patience. Then the beloved son - words this Gospel's readers have heard twice already, at the river and on the mountain - and the tenants say the quiet part aloud: this is the heir, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours. Which is the strangest logic in Scripture, since killing the son does not get them the vineyard; it only gets them the owner. And they threw him out of the vineyard and killed him, in that order, which is exactly where they took Him.

When the crowd reacts with the strongest negative in the Greek language, He looks at them and quotes Psalm 118 - the same psalm the disciples sang on the road seven verses earlier. They sang the blessing; He quotes the stone the builders threw away, and fuses Isaiah's stone of stumbling with Daniel's stone cut without hands.

Then the questions arrive like a relay. The spies pretend to be righteous, and every word of their flattery is true, which is what makes it dangerous. The tax question has no safe answer - people had died over that tax within living memory, and a Roman governor was in town for the feast. And the whole reply is contained in the first three words, before He says anything else: show me a denarius. He does not have one. It has to be produced by His questioners, in the temple, and it carried Tiberius's head with an inscription naming him son of the divine Augustus and high priest. Give back to Caesar what is his - his face is on it. And He never says what belongs to God, because He does not have to; if the coin belongs to Caesar because it carries his image, every person holding it knows what carries God's.

The Sadducees held only the books of Moses as binding and denied the resurrection, so their seven-brother riddle is not a question but a joke designed to make the resurrection look absurd. He refuses the premise - the age to come is not this age with more of the same - and then proves the resurrection out of Moses, because that is the only court they accept. At the bush, God said I am the God of Abraham, present tense, of men centuries in the ground. He is not the God of the dead but of the living. Even the scribes concede it, and after that nobody dares ask anything. So He asks one instead, out of Psalm 110: if David calls him Lord, how is he his son? And He never answers it. He leaves it hanging in the air of that temple, with the answer standing in front of them. The last word before the widow is a warning about men who love long robes and the best seats and who devour widows' houses.

verses.1: On one of those days, as he was teaching the people in the temple and preaching the Good News, the priests and scribes came to him with the elders.
verses.2: They asked him, “Tell us: by what authority do you do these things? Or who is giving you this authority?”
verses.3: He answered them, “I also will ask you one question. Tell me:
verses.4: the baptism of John, was it from heaven, or from men?”
verses.5: They reasoned with themselves, saying, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say, ‘Why didn’t you believe him?’
verses.6: But if we say, ‘From men,’ all the people will stone us, for they are persuaded that John was a prophet.”
verses.7: They answered that they didn’t know where it was from.
verses.8: Jesus said to them, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things.”
verses.9: He began to tell the people this parable. “A man planted a vineyard, and rented it out to some farmers, and went into another country for a long time.
verses.10: At the proper season, he sent a servant to the farmers to collect his share of the fruit of the vineyard. But the farmers beat him, and sent him away empty.
verses.11: He sent yet another servant, and they also beat him, and treated him shamefully, and sent him away empty.
verses.12: He sent yet a third, and they also wounded him, and threw him out.
verses.13: The lord of the vineyard said, ‘What shall I do? I will send my beloved son. It may be that seeing him, they will respect him.’
verses.14: “But when the farmers saw him, they reasoned among themselves, saying, ‘This is the heir. Come, let’s kill him, that the inheritance may be ours.’
verses.15: They threw him out of the vineyard, and killed him. What therefore will the lord of the vineyard do to them?
verses.16: He will come and destroy these farmers, and will give the vineyard to others.” When they heard it, they said, “May it never be!”
verses.17: But he looked at them, and said, “Then what is this that is written, ‘The stone which the builders rejected, the same was made the chief cornerstone?’
verses.18: Everyone who falls on that stone will be broken to pieces, but it will crush whomever it falls on to dust.”
verses.19: The chief priests and the scribes sought to lay hands on him that very hour, but they feared the people—for they knew he had spoken this parable against them.
verses.20: They watched him, and sent out spies, who pretended to be righteous, that they might trap him in something he said, so as to deliver him up to the power and authority of the governor.
verses.21: They asked him, “Teacher, we know that you say and teach what is right, and aren’t partial to anyone, but truly teach the way of God.
verses.22: Is it lawful for us to pay taxes to Caesar, or not?”
verses.23: But he perceived their craftiness, and said to them, “Why do you test me?
verses.24: Show me a denarius. Whose image and inscription are on it?” They answered, “Caesar’s.”
verses.25: He said to them, “Then give to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.”
verses.26: They weren’t able to trap him in his words before the people. They marveled at his answer, and were silent.
verses.27: Some of the Sadducees came to him, those who deny that there is a resurrection.
verses.28: They asked him, “Teacher, Moses wrote to us that if a man’s brother dies having a wife, and he is childless, his brother should take the wife, and raise up children for his brother.
verses.29: There were therefore seven brothers. The first took a wife, and died childless.
verses.30: The second took her as wife, and he died childless.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 21 - Two Small Coins, Not One Stone Left, and Lift Up Your Heads
chapters.title: Two Small Coins, Not One Stone Left, and Lift Up Your Heads
keyNotes: There is no chapter break in the original. He has just said the scribes devour widows' houses, and now He is watching a widow give her last two coins into the same system (Luke 21:1, 20:47).

The treasury was a set of trumpet-mouthed chests in the Court of the Women, and the amount was declared to the receiving priest. Giving was audible - which is what makes her two coins so quiet (Luke 21:1-2).
The lepton was the smallest coin in circulation. She had two, which means she could have kept one and nobody on earth would have blamed her (Luke 21:2).
"All that she had to live on" is bios - her living, her life. It is the same word Luke used for the estate the father divided between his sons (Luke 21:4, 15:12).
He does not stop her. He does not tell her to keep it. He commends her, and the next thing He says is that the whole building is coming down (Luke 21:4-6).
Herod's temple was still unfinished when He said this, and would only be completed about seven years before it was destroyed (Luke 21:5).
"Gifts" here are votive offerings hung in the courts - the most famous being a golden vine with clusters the height of a man (Luke 21:5).

They ask two questions - when, and what sign - and He answers with two horizons, the fall of the city and the end of the age, woven together. Much of the difficulty in this chapter is that we want them separated and He does not separate them (Luke 21:7).
The first instruction is not a sign to look for but a warning about people who bring you one: don't be led astray (Luke 21:8).
"The end won't come immediately." He applies the brake before He has described anything - the same brake He applied to the Kingdom appearing immediately two chapters ago (Luke 21:9, 19:11).
"But before all these things" puts the arrests and the trials first in the sequence. The persecution is not the last chapter; it is the first (Luke 21:12).
"It will turn out as a testimony for you" - martyrion. The dock becomes the pulpit, which is precisely what Acts spends its second half describing (Luke 21:13).
"Don't meditate beforehand how to answer" uses a rhetorical term for preparing a speech. He is telling them not to write the defence (Luke 21:14).
"I will give you a mouth and wisdom." Not notes - a mouth. The advocate promised is Himself (Luke 21:15).

"Not a hair of your head will perish" sits two verses after "some of you they will cause to be put to death." Both are said to the same people, so the preservation being promised is not physical survival (Luke 21:16, 18).
"By your endurance you will win your lives" - hupomone, which is not gritted teeth but remaining under a weight without moving (Luke 21:19).
Where Matthew and Mark have the abomination of desolation, Luke writes "Jerusalem surrounded by armies." He is writing for readers who need it in plain words (Luke 21:20).
"Let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains." Eusebius records that the Jerusalem believers left the city before the siege closed. The warning was given, and it was heeded (Luke 21:21).
"Days of vengeance, that all things which are written may be fulfilled" frames what is coming by Scripture rather than by Rome. The armies are not the authors (Luke 21:22).
"Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who nurse" is not a curse on mothers. It is compassion about how hard it will be to run (Luke 21:23).
"Until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled" states an interval, and an interval has an end. It is one of the most hope-carrying words in the chapter (Luke 21:24).
Sun, moon and stars darkened is standard prophetic language for the fall of powers - Joel and Isaiah both use it. Whether it is only figurative here, this book does not claim to know (Luke 21:25).
"The Son of Man coming in a cloud" is Daniel 7, and in Daniel that figure is coming toward the Ancient of Days to receive a kingdom (Luke 21:27).
"Look up, and lift up your heads" is the only instruction in the chapter about posture, and it is given for the worst moment in it (Luke 21:28).
"Your redemption" is apolutrosis - the ransom word, the price paid to bring someone out of slavery (Luke 21:28).
Luke's fig tree parable adds three words no one else has: and all the trees. That makes it hard to read the fig tree as a coded reference to one nation (Luke 21:29).

"This generation will not pass away" is the hardest sentence in the chapter. Genea can mean a generation of about forty years, or a kind of people. The city did fall within forty years, which fits the first sense; the language of verses 25 to 27 reaches beyond it. This book flags the difficulty rather than settling it (Luke 21:32).

"Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will by no means pass away" - and five chapters ago He said it was easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one stroke of the law to fall. He puts His words in the same category (Luke 21:33, 16:17).
The danger named in verse 34 is not tribulation. It is carousing, drunkenness, and the cares of this life - two of those are pleasant and one of them is just ordinary worry (Luke 21:34).
"Like a snare" - the word is for a trap that springs on a bird that never saw it (Luke 21:35).
The discourse ends in prayer, not in a calendar. Watch and pray that you may have strength to escape, and to stand (Luke 21:36).

The last two verses are the quietest in the chapter: teaching by day, sleeping on the Mount of Olives at night, and the whole city coming early in the morning to hear Him. That is the last picture before the Passover (Luke 21:37-38).

intro: There is no chapter break here. Our Bibles insert one, but the last thing said was that the scribes devour widows' houses - and then He looks up and sees a widow putting two coins into the treasury. Those two sentences belong together.

The treasury was thirteen trumpet-mouthed chests in the Court of the Women, and the amount was declared aloud to the receiving priest, which means giving was audible; wealth could be heard going in. Her two lepta were the smallest coins in circulation and could not be divided further. She had two, so she could have given one and kept one, and nobody would have thought less of her. All that she had to live on translates bios - her living, her life, the same word used for the estate the father divided between his sons.

And He does not stop her. That is the part worth sitting with. He knows exactly what the system is; He has just said what these men do to widows' houses. He lets her give, honours it, and says nothing to make her take it back.

Then somebody admires the building, which is fair - stones the size of rooms, and votive gifts hung in the courts including a golden vine with clusters as tall as a man. The building was not even finished; it would be completed about seven years before it was flattened. And He says not one stone will be left on another. They ask two questions, when and what sign, and He answers with two horizons - the city that will fall in their lifetime and the end of the age - woven together. Much of the difficulty of this chapter comes from wanting them separated with headings, which He does not supply.

The first instruction is not a sign to watch for but a warning about anyone who brings one. The first danger is not the war; it is the person who arrives with a date. And after listing wars, earthquakes, famines and plagues, He applies the brake before He has finished describing the car: the end will not be at once. Then before all these things - before - they will lay hands on you, and the persecution is placed first in the sequence rather than last. The dock becomes the pulpit, which is what the second half of Acts spends its time describing, and the defence is not to be written in advance, because the advocate promised is a mouth rather than a script.

Two verses have to be read together or they will wound: some of you they will put to death, and not a hair of your head will perish. Both, to the same people, in one breath - so what is promised is not survival but that nothing will be lost. Where Matthew and Mark have the abomination of desolation, Luke writes Jerusalem surrounded by armies, in plain words for readers who needed them plainly, and the believers in that city left before the siege closed. The trampling is given an expiry - until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled - and when the sun and moon fail and the powers of the heavens are shaken, the instruction given to His own is the opposite posture to everyone else's: look up, and lift up your heads, because your redemption is drawing near. Luke's fig tree adds three words nobody else has, and all the trees, which makes it hard to turn into a code about one nation. And the danger named at the end is not tribulation but carousing, drunkenness and the cares of this life - two pleasures and one ordinary worry, on the same list. The discourse ends in prayer rather than in a chart.

keyNotes: Luke runs the two names together - the feast of unleavened bread, which is called the Passover - because he is writing for readers who do not live inside the calendar (Luke 22:1).
"They feared the people." The entire timetable of the arrest is set by crowd control, and Judas is the solution to a scheduling problem (Luke 22:2, 6).
"Satan entered into Judas." Luke closed the wilderness temptation by saying the devil departed until an opportune time. This is that time, and Luke expects you to remember (Luke 22:3, 4:13).
"Who was counted with the twelve" is not filler. Luke keeps insisting on Judas's standing - he was one of them, fully (Luke 22:3, 47).
The captains Judas negotiates with are the strategoi, the officers of the temple police. This is arranged with temple security, not with Rome (Luke 22:4).
"The Passover must be sacrificed" - dei again, the word of divine necessity that Luke has used all the way through (Luke 22:7).
A man carrying a water jar was unusual enough to be a signal - that was normally a woman's task. The location stays unknown to Judas until they are already inside (Luke 22:10).
"With desire I have desired" is the literal Greek behind "I have earnestly desired" - a Hebrew intensive. He wanted this meal (Luke 22:15).
Luke has two cups: one shared before the bread, one after supper. That fits the Passover meal's sequence of cups rather than contradicting the other Gospels (Luke 22:17, 20).
"I will not drink again until God's Kingdom comes" is a vow of abstinence. He leaves the meal unfinished on purpose (Luke 22:16, 18).
"Do this in memory of me" - anamnesis is Passover vocabulary. Israel was already commanded to keep a memorial; He is putting Himself inside a rite they already knew (Luke 22:19).

The second half of verse 19 and all of verse 20 are missing from a few manuscripts. The WEB prints them, and so does nearly every English Bible. It is worth knowing that the argument exists (Luke 22:19-20).
"The new covenant in my blood" is Jeremiah's promise, and covenants in Torah are ratified by blood thrown against the people (Luke 22:20).
"The hand of him who betrays me is with me on the table" is Psalm 41 - a friend who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me (Luke 22:21).
Verse 22 holds two things together without softening either: the Son of Man goes as it has been determined, and woe to that man. Purpose does not cancel guilt (Luke 22:22).
The argument about who is the greatest happens at that table, minutes after the bread. Luke puts it there, and it is the most uncomfortable placement in the Gospel (Luke 22:24).
"Benefactors" was a real title. Hellenistic kings had it stamped on their coins. He is describing a public-relations exercise (Luke 22:25).
"I am among you as one who serves." Luke has no foot-washing scene; this sentence is where his account puts the same truth (Luke 22:27).
"I confer on you a kingdom" uses the verb for making a covenant or a will. He is drawing up a testament at a table on the night before He dies (Luke 22:29).
"Simon, Simon" - the doubled name again, as with Martha. It is tenderness before hard news (Luke 22:31, 10:41).
In verse 31 the "you" Satan asked for is plural - all of you. In verse 32 the "you" He prayed for is singular. English hides the change; the sifting was aimed at the whole group (Luke 22:31-32).
"That your faith wouldn't fail" - not that you would not fall. He does not pray Peter out of the failure; He prays him through it (Luke 22:32).
"When once you have turned again, establish your brothers." The restoration is spoken of as settled before the denial has even happened (Luke 22:32).
The swords are a reversal of the earlier sending, when they took nothing and lacked nothing. The world has changed around them (Luke 22:35-36).
"That is enough" almost certainly means enough of this, not two will do. Nobody arms a revolution with two swords, and an hour later He heals the only wound one of them causes (Luke 22:38, 51).
"He was counted with transgressors" is Isaiah 53, and He says it must be fulfilled in me. He reads His own death out of the prophets before it happens (Luke 22:37).
"As his custom was" to the Mount of Olives. That habit is exactly how Judas knew where to bring the crowd (Luke 22:39, 21:37).
The garden scene is bracketed by the same instruction - pray that you don't enter into temptation - said before and after. The prayer is the point of the passage (Luke 22:40, 46).

The angel and the sweat like drops of blood are absent from some early manuscripts and present in others. The WEB prints them. Note that Luke writes like great drops of blood - a comparison, not a diagnosis (Luke 22:43-44).
"Sleeping because of grief" is only in Luke. Of the three accounts, his is the one that makes an excuse for them (Luke 22:45).
The last words He speaks to Judas are his name and a question. No curse, no denunciation (Luke 22:48).
Luke, the physician, is the one who tells us the ear was healed. The final miracle before the cross repairs damage done by a friend, to an enemy (Luke 22:51).
"This is your hour, and the power of darkness." He gives the hour a name and an owner, and an hour is a limited thing (Luke 22:53).
Peter is sitting in the firelight, which is why the servant girl can look at him closely. Luke gives us the lighting (Luke 22:55-56).
"The Lord turned and looked at Peter" is in no other Gospel. The trial and the courtyard were the same building (Luke 22:61).
While they blindfold Him and demand he prophesy who struck Him, a prophecy He made hours earlier is coming true in the courtyard outside (Luke 22:64, 61).
"If I tell you, you won't believe" is a statement about them, not an evasion. Then He answers anyway, in the words of Psalm 110 (Luke 22:67-69).
"You say it, because I am." That is the sentence the council calls sufficient, and they are right - there is nothing left to ask (Luke 22:70-71).

intro: The last section of this Gospel begins with a betrayal being arranged in an office. The chief priests want Him dead and cannot work out how, because they are afraid of the crowd - and that is the only thing restraining them. Not law, not conscience. Logistics. Then Judas walks in and solves the problem.

Satan entered into him, and the reader is expected to remember something: when the devil left Him in the wilderness, the text said he departed until an opportune time. This is that time, and the book has held the thread for eighteen chapters. Luke also refuses to let Judas become a stranger, repeating that he was one of the twelve, counted among them. He was not an outsider who got in.

The upper room follows the pattern of the colt: go into the city, a man carrying a water jar will meet you, follow him. Carrying water was women's work, so the man is a signal, and a discreet one - not even the twelve know the address until they are standing in it, and a location that has not been given cannot be betrayed. And He sits down and says, in a Hebrew intensive that reads literally as with desire I have desired, that He wanted this Passover before He suffered. Whatever else is in that room, He is not being dragged into it.

He shares a cup and says He will not drink of the fruit of the vine again until the Kingdom comes, which is a vow. He leaves the meal unfinished on purpose. Then bread, and a memorial word that was already Passover vocabulary - they were keeping a memorial that night, of a lamb and a doorframe and a night of deliverance - and He steps inside a rite they already had and says it was always about Him. Then the cup after supper, and Jeremiah's new covenant, the one God promised to write on the inside of people.

And straight from that: the hand of the one who betrays me is with me on the table. Then a contention among them about which of them is the greatest - at that table, with the bread in their hands. He does not throw them out. He tells them what greatness is, and says that He is among them as one who serves.

Then Simon, and the doubled name that in this Gospel signals tenderness before hard news. Satan asked to have you, and in the Greek that you is plural - the sifting was aimed at the whole table. But I have prayed for you, and that one is singular. Not that Peter would avoid falling, since He says three sentences later that he will, but that the fall would not be the end - and Peter is given a job on the far side of it before he has failed. The swords that follow are often misread: two swords are not enough for anything, the most natural reading of it is enough is enough of this, and when one of them is actually drawn an hour later He undoes the damage. The garden gives details found nowhere else - a stone's throw, kneeling, an angel, sweat like great drops of blood, and the last two of those are missing from some of the oldest manuscripts, which this book will not hide. He asked for the cup to pass and then submitted, and both halves are in the prayer. Only Luke says the disciples were sleeping for sorrow. The last words to Judas are his name and a question. And the last miracle before the cross is an ear restored - done for a man who came to arrest Him, undoing harm caused by one of His own.

verses.1: Now the feast of unleavened bread, which is called the Passover, was approaching.
verses.2: The chief priests and the scribes sought how they might put him to death, for they feared the people.
verses.3: Satan entered into Judas, who was also called Iscariot, who was counted with the twelve.
verses.4: He went away, and talked with the chief priests and captains about how he might deliver him to them.
verses.5: They were glad, and agreed to give him money.
verses.6: He consented, and sought an opportunity to deliver him to them in the absence of the multitude.
verses.7: The day of unleavened bread came, on which the Passover must be sacrificed.
verses.8: Jesus sent Peter and John, saying, “Go and prepare the Passover for us, that we may eat.”
verses.9: They said to him, “Where do you want us to prepare?”
verses.10: He said to them, “Behold, when you have entered into the city, a man carrying a pitcher of water will meet you. Follow him into the house which he enters.
verses.11: Tell the master of the house, ‘The Teacher says to you, “Where is the guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?”’
verses.12: He will show you a large, furnished upper room. Make preparations there.”
verses.13: They went, found things as Jesus had told them, and they prepared the Passover.
verses.14: When the hour had come, he sat down with the twelve apostles.
verses.15: He said to them, “I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer,
verses.16: for I tell you, I will no longer by any means eat of it until it is fulfilled in God’s Kingdom.”
verses.17: He received a cup, and when he had given thanks, he said, “Take this, and share it among yourselves,
verses.18: for I tell you, I will not drink at all again from the fruit of the vine, until God’s Kingdom comes.”
verses.19: He took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke, and gave it to them, saying, “This is my body which is given for you. Do this in memory of me.”
verses.20: Likewise, he took the cup after supper, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood, which is poured out for you.
verses.21: But behold, the hand of him who betrays me is with me on the table.
verses.22: The Son of Man indeed goes, as it has been determined, but woe to that man through whom he is betrayed!”
verses.23: They began to question among themselves, which of them it was who would do this thing.
verses.24: There arose also a contention among them, which of them was considered to be greatest.
verses.25: He said to them, “The kings of the nations lord it over them, and those who have authority over them are called ‘benefactors.’
verses.26: But not so with you. But one who is the greater among you, let him become as the younger, and one who is governing, as one who serves.
verses.27: For who is greater, one who sits at the table, or one who serves? Isn’t it he who sits at the table? But I am among you as one who serves.
verses.28: But you are those who have continued with me in my trials.
verses.29: I confer on you a kingdom, even as my Father conferred on me,
verses.30: that you may eat and drink at my table in my Kingdom. You will sit on thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”
verses.31: The Lord said, “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan asked to have all of you, that he might sift you as wheat,
verses.32: but I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn’t fail. You, when once you have turned again, establish your brothers.”
verses.33: He said to him, “Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death!”
verses.34: He said, “I tell you, Peter, the rooster will by no means crow today until you deny that you know me three times.”
verses.35: He said to them, “When I sent you out without purse, and wallet, and shoes, did you lack anything?” They said, “Nothing.”
verses.36: Then he said to them, “But now, whoever has a purse, let him take it, and likewise a wallet. Whoever has none, let him sell his cloak, and buy a sword.
verses.37: For I tell you that this which is written must still be fulfilled in me: ‘He was counted with transgressors.’ For that which concerns me has an end.”
verses.38: They said, “Lord, behold, here are two swords.” He said to them, “That is enough.”
verses.39: He came out, and went, as his custom was, to the Mount of Olives. His disciples also followed him.
verses.40: When he was at the place, he said to them, “Pray that you don’t enter into temptation.”
verses.41: He was withdrawn from them about a stone’s throw, and he knelt down and prayed,
verses.42: saying, “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.”
verses.43: An angel from heaven appeared to him, strengthening him.
verses.44: Being in agony he prayed more earnestly. His sweat became like great drops of blood falling down on the ground.
verses.45: When he rose up from his prayer, he came to the disciples, and found them sleeping because of grief,
verses.46: and said to them, “Why do you sleep? Rise and pray that you may not enter into temptation.”
verses.47: While he was still speaking, behold, a multitude, and he who was called Judas, one of the twelve, was leading them. He came near to Jesus to kiss him.
verses.48: But Jesus said to him, “Judas, do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?”
verses.49: When those who were around him saw what was about to happen, they said to him, “Lord, shall we strike with the sword?”
verses.50: A certain one of them struck the servant of the high priest, and cut off his right ear.
verses.51: But Jesus answered, “Let me at least do this”—and he touched his ear, and healed him.
verses.52: Jesus said to the chief priests, captains of the temple, and elders, who had come against him, “Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs?
verses.53: When I was with you in the temple daily, you didn’t stretch out your hands against me. But this is your hour, and the power of darkness.”
verses.54: They seized him, and led him away, and brought him into the high priest’s house. But Peter followed from a distance.
verses.55: When they had kindled a fire in the middle of the courtyard, and had sat down together, Peter sat among them.
verses.56: A certain servant girl saw him as he sat in the light, and looking intently at him, said, “This man also was with him.”
verses.57: He denied Jesus, saying, “Woman, I don’t know him.”
verses.58: After a little while someone else saw him, and said, “You also are one of them!” But Peter answered, “Man, I am not!”
verses.59: After about one hour passed, another confidently affirmed, saying, “Truly this man also was with him, for he is a Galilean!”
verses.60: But Peter said, “Man, I don’t know what you are talking about!” Immediately, while he was still speaking, a rooster crowed.
verses.61: The Lord turned, and looked at Peter. Then Peter remembered the Lord’s word, how he said to him, “Before the rooster crows you will deny me three times.”
verses.62: He went out, and wept bitterly.
verses.63: The men who held Jesus mocked him and beat him.
verses.64: Having blindfolded him, they struck him on the face and asked him, “Prophesy! Who is the one who struck you?”
verses.65: They spoke many other things against him, insulting him.
verses.66: As soon as it was day, the assembly of the elders of the people were gathered together, both chief priests and scribes, and they led him away into their council, saying,
verses.67: “If you are the Christ, tell us.” But he said to them, “If I tell you, you won’t believe,
verses.68: and if I ask, you will in no way answer me or let me go.
verses.69: From now on, the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God.”
verses.70: They all said, “Are you then the Son of God?” He said to them, “You say it, because I am.”
verses.71: They said, “Why do we need any more witness? For we ourselves have heard from his own mouth!”

cites.text: and you shall keep it until the fourteenth day of the same month; and the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel shall kill it at evening.
You shall sacrifice the Passover to Yahweh your God, of the flock and the herd, in the place which Yahweh shall choose, to cause his name to dwell there.

7.why: the lamb killed at evening by the whole assembly, and the Passover sacrificed at the place he chooses

cites.text: This day shall be to you for a memorial, and you shall keep it a feast to Yahweh: throughout your generations you shall keep it a feast by an ordinance forever.

You shall tell your son in that day, saying, ‘It is because of that which Yahweh did for me when I came out of Egypt.’ It shall be for a sign to you on your hand, and for a memorial between your eyes, that Yahweh’s law may be in your mouth; for with a strong hand Yahweh has brought you out of Egypt.

19.why: a day to be kept as a memorial, and telling your son what Yahweh did for you

cites.text: “Behold, the days come,” says Yahweh, “that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah: not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers in the day that I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt; which covenant of mine they broke, although I was a husband to them,” says Yahweh. “But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days,” says Yahweh: I will put my law in their inward parts, and I will write it in their heart. I will be their God, and they shall be my people.
Moses took the blood, and sprinkled it on the people, and said, “Look, this is the blood of the covenant, which Yahweh has made with you concerning all these words.”

20.why: the new covenant written on the heart, and the blood of the covenant thrown on the people

cites.text: Yes, my own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, who ate bread with me, has lifted up his heel against me.

For it was not an enemy who insulted me, then I could have endured it. Neither was it he who hated me who raised himself up against me, then I would have hidden myself from him. But it was you, a man like me, my companion, and my familiar friend. We took sweet fellowship together. We walked in God’s house with company.

21.why: my own familiar friend who ate my bread lifted his heel, and it was not an enemy but a companion

cites.text: He said, “This will be the way of the king who shall reign over you: he will take your sons, and appoint them as his servants, for his chariots, and to be his horsemen; and they will run before his chariots. He will appoint them to him for captains of thousands, and captains of fifties; and he will assign some to plow his ground, and to reap his harvest, and to make his instruments of war, and the instruments of his chariots. He will take your daughters to be perfumers, to be cooks, and to be bakers. He will take your fields, your vineyards, and your olive groves, even their best, and give them to his servants. He will take one tenth of your seed, and of your vineyards, and give it to his officers, and to his servants. He will take your male servants, your female servants, your best young men, and your donkeys, and assign them to his own work. He will take one tenth of your flocks; and you will be his servants. You will cry out in that day because of your king whom you will have chosen for yourselves; and Yahweh will not answer you in that day.”

“Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel. Prophesy, and tell them, even the shepherds, ‘Thus says the Lord Yahweh: “Woe to the shepherds of Israel who feed themselves! Shouldn’t the shepherds feed the sheep? You eat the fat. You clothe yourself with the wool. You kill the fatlings, but you don’t feed the sheep. You haven’t strengthened the diseased. You haven’t healed that which was sick. You haven’t bound up that which was broken. You haven’t brought back that which was driven away. You haven’t sought that which was lost, but you have ruled over them with force and with rigor.

25.why: what a king will take from you, and shepherds who feed themselves and not the flock

cites.text: But the saints of the Most High will receive the kingdom, and possess the kingdom forever, even forever and ever.’
where the tribes go up, even Yah’s tribes, according to an ordinance for Israel, to give thanks to Yahweh’s name. For there are set thrones for judgment, the thrones of David’s house.

29.why: the saints receiving the kingdom, and thrones set for judgment in the house of David

cites.text: Then Satan answered Yahweh, and said, “Does Job fear God for nothing? Haven’t you made a hedge around him, and around his house, and around all that he has, on every side? You have blessed the work of his hands, and his substance is increased in the land. But stretch out your hand now, and touch all that he has, and he will renounce you to your face.” Yahweh said to Satan, “Behold, all that he has is in your power. Only on himself don’t stretch out your hand.” So Satan went out from the presence of Yahweh.
“For, behold, I will command, and I will sift the house of Israel among all the nations, as grain is sifted in a sieve, yet not the least kernel will fall on the earth.

31.why: the accuser asking permission, and Israel sifted among the nations without one grain falling

cites.text: Therefore will I give him a portion with the great, and he will divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was counted with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
They made his grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in his death; although he had done no violence, nor was any deceit in his mouth.

37.why: numbered with the transgressors and bearing the sin of many, and made his grave with the wicked

cites.text: Awake, awake! Stand up, Jerusalem, you who have drunk from Yahweh’s hand the cup of his wrath. You have drunken the bowl of the cup of staggering, and drained it.
I delight to do your will, my God. Yes, your law is within my heart.”

42.why: the cup of his wrath drunk to the dregs, and I delight to do your will, my God

cites.text: Yes, my own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, who ate bread with me, has lifted up his heel against me.

“Awake, sword, against my shepherd, and against the man who is close to me,” says Yahweh of Armies. “Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered; and I will turn my hand against the little ones.

48.why: the friend who lifted his heel, and strike the shepherd and the sheep will be scattered
